items.title: Scotland’s Scott splits Australian swim dominance at Commonwealths
items.summary: Scotland’s Scott splits Australian swim dominance at Commonwealths
items.body_text:
Scotland's Scott splits Australian swim dominance at Commonwealths
- By AFP -
- Jul 25, 2026
Duncan Scott delivered hosts Scotland’s first gold medal of the Commonwealth Games to break up Australia’s dominance of the pool on the first full day of action in Glasgow on Friday.
With the programme nearly halved to just 10 sports, swimming is the highlight of the schedule across the opening weekend.
Scott set a Games record of 1min 56.38sec to win the 200-metre individual medley from New Zealand’s Lewis Clareburt and England’s Thomas Dean.
The 29-year-old now has four Commonwealth golds and 14 medals in total.
“It was a tough one because you really want to give the team some good momentum early doors and being one of the senior members of the team, the onus was on me,” said Scott.
“I was a bit nervous before that. Those boys made it tough, but I’m happy with that. It’s a good way to start the meet.”
Elsewhere, Australia’s green and gold topped the podium, with an extra bonus for those who emerged victorious.
Mining baron Gina Rinehart, Australia’s richest person, is funding an incentive scheme of 20,000 Australian dollars ($14,000) for every gold medal and 30,000 Australian dollars for breaking a world record.
Aussie swimmers dominated in Birmingham four years ago, taking home nearly half of the 52 gold medals on offer, and won four of the five finals on opening night.
Lani Pallister was first to cash in as she led an Australian 1-2-3 in the women’s 400m freestyle.
Jenna Forrester took bronze in the first medal race of the night and then denied Katie Shanahan a Scottish gold to narrowly edge the women’s 200m backstroke.
Australia led home England and South Africa in both the men’s and women’s 4x100m freestyle races.
The Australian men’s team of Flynn Southam, Kai Taylor, Harrison Turner and Kyle Chalmers set a new Games record of 3mins 09.49sec.
By securing South Africa’s bronze on the final leg of the men’s race, Chad le Clos set a record with his 19th Commonwealth medal, more than any other male athlete.
Adam Ramsay-Peaty cruised into the final of the men’s 100m breaststroke back at the scene of his first international medals at the 2014 Games.
The three-time Olympic gold medallist set the fastest time in the semi-finals.
– Canada win disrupted gymnastics –
Canada claimed gold in the men’s gymnastics team final, but the event was overshadowed by a sickening fall for England’s Gabriel Langton.
England were second heading into the final apparatus on the high bar when Langton slipped off and came down head first.
The 19-year-old was able to move his arms and legs before being carefully stretchered away from the arena, but the competition was held up for 20 minutes as he received medical attention.
The fall also allowed Canada to ease to gold, with England taking silver and Australia edging out Scotland for bronze.
“It was really tough. We just had to reset, try to put it to one side mentally and focus on the job we had to do. I think everyone should be proud of the way we carried on after Gabe’s fall,” said England’s Luke Whitehouse.
Mark Swan won the first gold of the Games with a dramatic victory in the men’s lightweight category of the para powerlifting.
Swan thought he had come up short after failing with his final lift, but he had in fact topped the standings ahead of Nigeria’s Roland Ezuruike by the slimmest of margins, based on a coefficient related to body weight.
Swan lifted 222kg, more than three times his body weight, with his second lift, but said: “I came back off the third lift and thought, ‘Well, I’ve got bronze’. My coach said ‘good job on gold’. I thought he was winding me up!”
Nigeria dominated the other para powerlifting events with three golds, including a world record of 175kg for Folashade Oluwafemiayo in the heavyweight division.

items.title: Despite Haas struggles, youthful Bearman believes he can win
items.summary: Despite Haas struggles, youthful Bearman believes he can win
items.body_text:
Despite Haas struggles, youthful Bearman believes he can win
- By AFP -
- Jul 25, 2026
Oliver Bearman has made a spotty start to his Formula One career, but he told AFP he has “what it takes to become a world champion”, hopefully for Ferrari.
At just 21, the Englishman started his second full season strongly for Haas, with top-10 finishes in the first two races but has since picked up only one more point.
Part of a quintet of youngsters in the paddock, Bearman trails behind Franco Colapinto and Isack Hadjar, in their early twenties, as well as 18-year-old Arvid Lindblad.
But they have all been overshadowed by Kimi Antonelli, who turns 20 next month and tops the driver standings with more points than the other four put together.
Talking exclusively to AFP, Bearman said that having competed with Antonelli at youth level, he is encouraged by the Italian’s success.
“I raced alongside Kimi. I was comparing myself with him for one year,” said Bearman.
“He’s racing in the World Championship fight, so that gives me confidence that one day, if I have the best car, I can do the same.
“I know I have what it takes to become a world champion.”
Nonetheless, Bearman conceded that “there’s a lot of external factors which are out of the driver’s hands”.
“There’s been lots of drivers who are deserving of a world champion who never got it,” the Chelmsford native said.
“I have the confidence in myself that I have what it takes.
“If you don’t have that, then you shouldn’t turn up to the track.”
He said he is progressing as a driver even though Haas are battling to stay competitive.
“We started incredibly strong, which is a really cool moment for the team and everybody. In terms of personal performance, I feel like I’m in a really good place. I’m really happy with what I’m doing,” Bearman said.
Bearman joined the Ferrari driver academy aged 16. At 18, he became the Scuderia’s youngest Formula One driver when he finished seventh in Saudi Arabia in 2024. Later that season he raced twice for Ferrari-powered Haas, recording a pair of top-10 finishes.
Last season, Bearman became a full-time Haas driver. The high point was fourth place in Mexico which, in the team’s 11th season, was one of their best ever finishes.
The Belgian Grand Prix in Spa-Francorchamps last weekend was the 10th of potentially 24 scheduled races this season.
“I see a good amount of evolution, a good amount of growth,” he said.
“If I compare what I was doing, my mindset heading into Spa last year versus this year, I’m a much more complete driver. I’ve learned so much. I understand my place within the team. I understand how to get the most out of the team and the most out of myself as well.”
‘Love to drive in red again’
In the new hybrid-car era, with teams continually updating their cars as they grapple with the technological challenges, Bearman said that mid-table rivals Racing Bulls, Alpine and Audi “seem to have jumped ahead of us”.
“It’s also a big motivator for us to keep pushing,” he said.
“After the summer break, we have some more stuff coming and hopefully that can get us back to where we started this season.
“I feel like I’m performing at a really good level, but the car is not giving me what it takes to get in the points.”
As Formula One approaches its annual game of musical car seats, Bearman’s future is uncertain.
“I don’t have a contract for next year. It’s tough on one hand because it’s not nice to be unsure about what the future holds,” he said, adding: “I’m deserving of a seat in Formula 1.
“I have had a lot of trust put in me by Ferrari who put me here.
“I would love to drive in red again one day.”

items.title: Lyles wins US 100m title in world-leading 9.79sec
items.summary: Lyles wins US 100m title in world-leading 9.79sec
items.body_text:
Lyles wins US 100m title in world-leading 9.79sec
- By AFP -
- Jul 25, 2026
Olympic gold medallist Noah Lyles powered to his third US 100m title in a world-leading 9.79sec on Friday at the US athletics championships.
Lyles, trailing at the start, surged over the final 30 meters for a convincing victory over veteran Ronnie Baker, who edged Kenny Bednarek for second.
Both were credited with a time of 9.88, with Bednarek taking third. Former world champion Christian Coleman came in fourth in 9.93.
“In my head, the distance was already made up,” Lyles told broadcaster NBC of the early gap he erased. “Coach said ‘put my hand in their pocket, don’t let ’em get away.’
“I saw where Christian was and I said: ‘Oh yeah, my hand is all the way in there,’ and I just pulled him back and I did what I do,” added Lyles.
He matched the personal best he set in winning Olympic gold in Paris in 2024 and improved on the previous world leading time this year of 9.82 set by Oblique Seville at the Jamaican championships in June.
Sha’Carri Richardson, the 2023 world champion and 2024 Olympic silver medallist, clocked 10.77sec (wind 0.9m/sec) to win her third national 100m title.
The 26-year-old Texan, whose difficult 2025 campaign saw her finish off the podium in her 100m world championship defense, pulled away relentlessly from training partner Kayla White, who finished second in 10.90.
Tamari Davis was third in 11.00.
“It just feels phenomenal to be back in a better place, just healthy mentally, physically and emotionally,” Richardson said. “Everything me and coach have been working on, it’s starting to show consistently.”
Lyles will be back in action Saturday in the 200m heats.
In a year with no World Championships or Olympic team berths on the line, some well-known names opted out of the national championships or tweaked their programs at Icahn Stadium in New York City.
Melissa Jefferson-Wooden, who swept 100m, 200m and 4x100m gold at last September’s World Championships, skipped the 100m and will launch her campaign in the 200m heats on Saturday.
Quincy Hall, the 400m gold medallist at the 2024 Paris Olympics, failed to advance from the heats as his 46.47 left him in 16th place in a field led by Khaleb McRae’s 44.65.
Cooper Lutkenhaus, the 17-year-old sensation who has bagged two Diamond League victories this year in his first season on the elite circuit, moved safely into the men’s 800m final, winning his heat in 1:45.83.
Lutkenhaus clocked the third-fastest time of the first round, led by Wes Ferguson’s 1:45.17.
Donovan Brazier, the 2019 world champion who held off Lutkenhaus to capture the national title last year, failed to advance.

items.title: Trump makes long-awaited return to Correspondents’ Dinner
items.summary: President delivers joke-filled speech while addressing politics, Iran and press relations. The post Trump makes long-awaited return to Correspondents’ Dinner appeared first on BOL News.
items.body_text:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump turned the White House Correspondents’ Association (WHCA) Dinner into a mix of comedy and politics on Friday, delivering jokes, media jabs and remarks on key national and international issues during his long-awaited return to the annual event.
The dinner, originally scheduled for April, was postponed after a gunman opened fire outside the Washington Hilton, forcing the evacuation of guests. Nearly three months later, the event was held under heightened security at the Waldorf Astoria, marking Trump’s first appearance at the correspondents’ dinner as president.
Opening his hour-long speech, Trump acknowledged the April shooting, saying the event could have ended in tragedy before adding that “the show must go on.” He also revealed that he had removed some of the harsher remarks from the speech originally prepared for the April gathering.
Throughout his address, Trump mixed humor with criticism, taking aim at journalists, political rivals and celebrities. His targets included former President Barack Obama, California Governor Gavin Newsom, Representative Ilhan Omar, television hosts Jimmy Kimmel and Jimmy Fallon, and entertainers Bruce Springsteen and Jane Fonda.
He also joked about the journalism awards presented during the evening, many of which recognised reporting critical of his administration.
The president briefly addressed the ongoing conflict involving Iran, saying diplomatic efforts remained underway while stressing that the United States remained prepared to escalate military action if necessary.
Read More: Trump confirms attendance as White House Correspondents’ Dinner gets new date
He said there was both a military and diplomatic path forward, adding that Washington remained “locked and loaded” while continuing talks.
Trump also joked about the possibility of serving a third presidential term before quickly clarifying that he was “only kidding.” Later in the evening, he drew laughter by putting on a red “Trump 2028” cap, calling it the night’s “scoop.”
One of the evening’s most talked-about moments came when Trump unexpectedly mentioned rapper Nicki Minaj while recalling the April shooting.
The remark quickly went viral on social media, drawing mixed reactions, with some users criticising it as insensitive while others praised the president’s comedic style.
Despite repeatedly criticising the media during his remarks, Trump ended on a conciliatory note, saying he respected journalism and believed in a free press.
He also defended his administration’s frequent engagement with reporters, arguing that direct interaction gives the public an opportunity to hear the government’s position firsthand.
Earlier in the evening, outgoing WHCA President Weijia Jiang said the decision to reschedule the dinner reflected the media’s determination not to be intimidated by political violence. She reaffirmed the association’s commitment to protecting press freedom and supporting independent journalism.
The White House Correspondents’ Association also honoured Secret Service officer Victor Gonzales, who was wounded while confronting the gunman during the April attack, as well as staff members of the Washington Hilton for their response during the incident.
The annual dinner, which has been held for more than a century, raises funds for journalism scholarships while celebrating the role of a free press.
This year’s gathering took place under significantly tighter security, with reduced attendance, multiple security checkpoints and enhanced law enforcement measures following the April shooting.
The event came amid continuing tensions between the Trump administration and several media organisations over lawsuits, press access and broader concerns about press freedom.
While critics have accused the administration of increasing pressure on the media, Trump has defended his approach, saying it is intended to promote accountability and address perceived bias.
Concluding his remarks, Trump thanked the audience

items.body_text:
Hernandez shares ’72 Hours’ experience with Kevin Hart
				
				
					
The movie was filmed in Miami, Hernandez's hometown.
				
		
				 
				
					Kevin Hart’s new Netflix comedy, “72 Hours,” is attracting attention for its star-studded cast and entertaining performances. However, critics remain divided over the film’s overall quality. Despite the mixed reviews, the comedy continues to generate buzz online.
Co-star Marcello Hernandez praised Kevin Hart’s professionalism and sense of humor. He said working with the comedian was both enjoyable and inspiring.
Hernandez joked that Hart taught him more than acting during filming. According to him, Hart shared lessons about dealing with back pain, sciatica and the challenges of getting older. “Hart taught me a lot of stuff,” Hernandez said. “He taught me how to deal with back pain and how to deal with sciatica. He also taught me that stairs become a challenge as you get older.”
Behind the jokes, Hernandez said he developed a deep respect for Hart’s work ethic. He described the actor as a true professional and said watching him work was one of the best parts of filming. “It was a blessing to see him work,” Hernandez said. “He is a true pro.”
The movie was filmed in Miami, Hernandez’s hometown. He said filming close to home made the experience even more special because he was able to spend time with his family. “It was a lot of work, but I got to stay with my mom,” he said. “Being close to my family while filming was a blessing.”
“72 Hours” follows an advertising executive played by Hart. After being mistakenly added to a group chat, he joins a group of younger men on a bachelor party trip to Miami. Hoping to better understand younger consumers, he offers to pay for the trip. His decision leads to a series of funny and chaotic situations.
It was directed by Tim Story, known for “Barbershop” and “Ride Along.” The screenplay was written by Jon Hurwitz and Hayden Schlossberg, the writers behind the “Harold & Kumar” film series. Many viewers have praised the cast’s chemistry and energetic performances.

items.body_text:
JD.com partners with Iraq’s GINI to expand e-commerce offerings
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – China’s JD.com has partnered with Iraqi digital commerce platform GINI to increase access to its goods in Iraq, marking the latest step toward developing the country’s rapidly expanding e-commerce industry.
The deal would integrate JD.com’s product catalog into GINI’s digital marketplace and the SuperQi app, providing Iraqi customers with greater access to items from one of China’s top online retailers.
The agreement aims to establish a direct supply chain between JD.com and the Iraqi market, thereby enhancing product availability and facilitating cross-border online buying.
GINI, an Iraqi digital commerce and market automation platform, combines merchants, delivery providers, and payment services in a unified ecosystem, allowing companies to manage sales, payments, and logistics.
JD.com, founded in 1998, is China’s largest retailer by revenue and one of the country’s leading e-commerce companies, with a vast logistics network that enables rapid order fulfillment across China and international markets.
The agreement comes as Iraq’s e-commerce sector grows, along with rising internet penetration, digital payment adoption, and government efforts to modernize the economy and encourage more private sector investment in technology and digital services.
Baghdad has increasingly pushed to recruit multinational technology businesses and digital commerce platforms as part of larger attempts to diversify the economy away from oil, generate private-sector employment, and enhance access to products and services via online markets.

items.title: Houthis say hit Saudi Arabia as Trump weighs harder Iran strikes
items.summary: Tehran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on Saudi Arabia on Saturday as US President Donald Trump mulled fresh strikes on Iran in the... The post Houthis say hit Saudi Arabia as Trump weighs harder Iran strikes appeared first on Iraqi News.
items.body_text:
Houthis say hit Saudi Arabia as Trump weighs harder Iran strikes
Sanaa – Tehran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile attack on Saudi Arabia on Saturday as US President Donald Trump mulled fresh strikes on Iran in the deepening Middle East war.
The US military broke its daily announcement of fresh strikes on the Islamic republic on Saturday, following 13 nights in a row hitting military targets there.
Trump said he had not yet decided whether to launch major strikes on Iran, hours before the conflict widened across the region with Yemen’s Houthi rebels claiming a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan.
The Houthis had accused US ally Riyadh of a “dangerous escalation” after it struck military targets belonging to the group on Friday, following the rebels announcing a maritime blockade of the top oil producer and hitting its ships in the Red Sea.
The flare-up marks a new front in a war that has engulfed the region following US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in February, and comes on top of Iran’s parallel blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Riyadh’s only other maritime route.
Riyadh did not immediately comment on the Houthis’ Ansarollah media post on Telegram on Saturday that a “Yemeni missile strike” had sparked fires in Jizan.
But Riyadh’s civil defence agency issued brief warnings to residents in the city, as well as Yanbu, early on Saturday.
The warning came after the Saudi-led coalition said Friday it had hit Houthi sites and destroyed targets threatening commercial vessels in response to attacks on Red Sea shipping.
A Yemeni security source told AFP a naval base in the port city of Hodeida and a military camp on Kamaran island were among the Saudi targets.
The Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi ships earlier this week, with Saudi Arabia confirming one of the attacks in the Red Sea.
– ‘Tipping point’ –
The escalation came after Trump said he would hold off on a major operation as Tehran was now getting “serious” in talks with Washington.
“No I haven’t,” Trump told journalists in the Oval Office when asked if he had made a decision on hitting Iran hard, for now dialing back reports that he was increasingly frustrated with the war and mulling a large-scale military operation.
“Look, we’re talking to them right now. I think they’re getting more and more serious as the days go by, for maybe the obvious reason.”
Trump said Iran had a choice between making a deal or facing a “much higher level” of strikes, after nearly two weeks of US attacks that have left a ceasefire in tatters.
The war that Trump once predicted would last four or five weeks is now nearing its fifth month, and is weighing on the Republican’s approval ratings ahead of crucial US midterm elections in November.
Trump added that he did not know what the “tipping point” would be for a decision, but reiterated that his red line would be if Iran was close to developing a nuclear weapon.
The United States says it is carrying out the strikes to stop Iran closing the crucial Strait of Hormuz.
Iran has responded with strikes on US bases that have killed four service members.
The Iranian military said Friday it had carried out attacks targeting US military assets in Bahrain, Jordan and Kuwait.
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, meanwhile, said they had targeted an Amazon data center in Bahrain, according to state media, though neither the US tech giant nor Bahrain has commented on the claim.
There was also no confirmation from the United States of any targeting of its facilities or personnel.
In Bahrain, sirens sounded again early Saturday, the interior ministry said, urging residents to take shelter.
– ‘I trust them’ –
Trump also insisted Russia and China were not arming Iran, despite reports both were feeding Tehran intelligence to target US forces.
“President Xi (Jinping) said he will not partake, and President (Vladimir) Putin said the same thing… I trust them,” Trump told reporters.
“I don’t think they’d want to have me disappointed.”
On the diplomatic front, Chine

items.body_text:
Houthis claim strike on Saudi Arabia as conflict deepens
Sanaa – Iran-backed Houthi rebels claimed a missile strike on Saudi Arabia on Saturday, hours after vowing to retaliate against the kingdom for attacks as the Middle East war expanded.
Riyadh struck Houthi military targets in Hodeida on Friday, with rebel media reporting two wounded after the Yemeni group announced a maritime blockade of the top oil producer and hit its ships.
The flare-up marks a new front of the war that has engulfed the region following US-Israeli strikes on Tehran in February, and comes on top of Iran’s parallel blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, Riyadh’s only other maritime route.
The rebels had accused Saudi Arabia of a “dangerous escalation” and said its actions “will not go unanswered”.
The Houthis’ Ansarollah media said on Telegram early Saturday that a “Yemeni missile strike” had sparked fires in the southern Saudi city of Jizan on the Red Sea.
Saudi Arabia did not immediately comment on the claim.
But Riyadh’s civil defence agency had issued brief warnings to residents in Jizan and Yanbu early Saturday for “potential danger”, only to lift the warnings minutes later.
Similar warnings have been issued in the past when missiles or drones were fired at the kingdom.
The warning came after the Saudi-led coalition said Friday it had hit Houthi sites and destroyed targets threatening commercial vessels in response to attacks on Red Sea shipping.
A Yemeni security source told AFP a naval base in the port city of Hodeida and a military camp on Kamaran island were among the Saudi targets.
The Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi ships earlier this week, with Saudi Arabia confirming one of the attacks in the Red Sea.
– Blockade –
The Yemeni security source, who requested anonymity, said the Saudi strikes targeted a telecommunications building near Hodeida’s port and a naval base at Ras al-Kathib in Hodeida.
The Houthis’ al-Masirah television channel said two people were wounded — a worker in Hodeida and a woman on Kamaran island.
It said a telecoms building had been hit in Hodeida.
On Monday, the rebels had warned in a radio message to ships that they would target vessels “belonging to (the) Saudi enemy” that do not comply with their blockade.
Saudi state media cited a transport authority official on Friday as saying “the vessel (NCC MASA), belonging to a Saudi company, was targeted while sailing in the Red Sea today… resulting in minor damage to the vessel’s hull”.
The ship resumed its course, the SPA added.
Red Sea access has become vital for Saudi Arabia to keep shipping oil as traffic in Hormuz is disrupted.
In April and May, all of Saudi seaborne crude exports departed from its Red Sea port of Yanbu, according to Kpler data. It represented 92 percent of all seaborne crude exports in June and 78 percent so far in July.
The Houthis have been at war with Yemen’s government since 2014, in a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands of people.
The recent exchange of fire threatens a 2022 truce that has held despite expiring.

items.title: Trump bombed at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner — and proved its point
items.summary: President Donald Trump bombed at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner Friday night. He knew he was bombing, too, and he even tried to meta-joke his way out of it. But no. Even the president’s jokes about his bad jokes fell flat, and he was widely ridiculed for the comedy routine afterward. Members of the media … The post Trump bombed at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner — and proved its point appeared first on Egypt Independent.
items.body_text:
President Donald Trump bombed at the White House Correspondents’ Dinner Friday night. He knew he was bombing, too, and he even tried to meta-joke his way out of it.
But no. Even the president’s jokes about his bad jokes fell flat, and he was widely ridiculed for the comedy routine afterward.
Members of the media mocking the leader’s dismal performance on live TV and all across the internet? In some other countries, that’s a criminal offense. But in the US, it’s the norm, so maybe Trump’s speech unwittingly underscored the theme of the dinner: America’s robust First Amendment protections.
In a rambling hour-long speech, Trump insulted journalists by name, repurposed old nicknames for political opponents, made a strange number of fat jokes that weren’t funny at all, and sounded mad at his unnamed writers for giving him weak material to work with. “Does anyone understand this stuff?” he said at one point, and the answer was generally no.
Some of Trump’s remarks were “vicious,” as press secretary Karoline Leavitt promised. But more than anything, the speech was just… boring.
And boring is one thing Trump never, ever wants to be. He claimed to be singlehandedly keeping the news business afloat, commenting, “When I’m gone, you’re all going to be broke.”
“Nobody gives a damn about anybody else,” he said, and proceeded to count how many stories on The New York Times front page are about him.
Trump’s low energy led more than one TV executive to muse that the president had stumbled upon a new technique against the media: Tank the ratings with a snoozefest.
Some attendees said they were surprised that Trump didn’t bring more original material, given how highly anticipated the dinner was, in part because his attendance ended his years-long boycott of the White House Correspondents’ Association’s annual fundraiser.
Friday’s dinner was a smaller-scale redo of the April 26 black-tie affair that was postponed after a gunman tried to rush into the ballroom of the Washington Hilton hotel.
The do-over dinner was held across town at the Waldorf Astoria, a building Trump once operated as his namesake DC hotel — and an unofficial clubhouse for his first administration.
“See those beautiful chandeliers? I can tell you everything about them,” he threatened.
Trump did strike some notes of unity, praising the Secret Service and denouncing political violence. “In this country, we believe in freedom of speech,” he said. “We settle our differences not with bullets, but with open and vigorous debate. And no deranged loser with a gun will ever change that.”
Then he joked about dinnergoers wearing bulletproof vests under their fancy outfits, “which many people didn’t want to wear because they’d rather die than look 20 pounds heavier.”
Trump covets control of media
Trump’s remarks showed how he understands the power of the press — and that he gets angry when he can’t control it. He singled out several CNN journalists by name.
In response, CNN CEO Mark Thompson said in a statement, “We stand by our journalists and the integrity and fairmindedness with which the CNN team reports the news. Honest, accurate journalism may sometimes irritate politicians, but our right to report and present that reporting to the public without government interference is fully protected by the US Constitution. CNN will continue to exercise this right.”
Trump also gave shoutouts to media executives whom he views as allies, namely Larry and David Ellison, who took control of Paramount last year and are now trying to buy Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN’s parent company. Paramount suffered a major setback earlier on Friday when it agreed to accept a months-long delay to the merger while legal challenges are resolved.
Invoking the fact that Paramount owns CBS News, Trump said David Ellison is “going to make, I think, fantastic changes and keep some of the great stuff going.”
Trump also made a convoluted joke about the controversial changes implemented by Ellison’s handpicked editor-in-chief

The fire in rural Guadalajara comes less than two weeks after a deadly blaze devastated a small expat community in southern Spain. items.body_text:
Firefighters in central Spain battled a wildfire on Wednesday that has burned more than 32,000 hectares (79,000 acres) in one of the country’s largest blazes on record.
The fire in rural Guadalajara comes less than two weeks after a deadly blaze devastated a small expat community in southern Spain. That small but extremely virulent fire killed 13 people, including several foreigners, in one of the southern European country’s deadliest wildfires.
Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez on Wednesday visited the fire-ravaged area in Guadalajara, and called for a pact between political parties to fight climate change.
“Year after year we clearly see how climate change kills and destroys wealth in our communities,” Sánchez said in the village of Tamajón, located less than two hours by car northeast of Madrid. “This isn’t politics. It is science, it’s about facts.”
Some 34 villages have been evacuated in the area but there are no reported serious injuries or deaths. More than 200 firefighters were supported by land vehicles and aircraft on Wednesday.
Spain this year has already suffered 22 major forest fires, defined as a fire that burns more than 500 hectares (1,235 acres.)
The Socialist leader said more than 100,000 hectares (247,000 acres) had already been scorched through the first half of the year, matching the total yearly average for Spain over the last decade.
Spain’s Minister for Ecological Transition, Sara Aagesen, described the Guadalajara fire as “one of the largest in the recent history of our country” and the largest ever for the region of Castilla La Mancha.
The Guadalajara blaze is the second-largest on record in Spain’s history after some 37,000 hectares (91,000 acres) were burned last year in the northwest of the country, according to data from the ecological transition ministry, as cited by EFE news agency.
Regional authorities said firefighters supported by water-dumping aircraft had so far protected homes in all 40 villages in the burned area, 90% of which belongs to a national park. Firefighters hope to have the nearly week-old fire under control by Friday, said Emiliano García-Page, regional president of Castilla La Mancha.
Miguel Ángel Moreno, mayor of the village of Zarzuela de Jadraque, said its 100 residents were evacuated Friday, with 14 taking refuge at a Red Cross shelter.
Moreno said that the firefighters should receive as much admiration as the soccer players who won the World Cup on Sunday.
The firefighters “had to run from one side of the village to the other putting out fires,” Moreno told Spanish national television TVE. “Besides the heroes who won the World Cup, we have other heroes who remain nameless.”
New heat wave could complicate firefighting efforts
Spain’s weather agency said a heat wave that began Tuesday was expected to reach its peak between Wednesday and Thursday, with temperatures pushing 40 degrees Celsius (104 Fahrenheit) in several inland areas and crossing 42 Celsius (108 Fahrenheit) in parts of Andalusia, in southern Spain.
Guadalajara and large areas of Spain were under alert for high temperatures.
Like many other European countries, Spain is experiencing extreme heat, which is combining with wind and limited rainfall to create ideal conditions for small wildfires to grow unchecked.
Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent, with temperatures increasing twice as quickly as the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service.
Globally, 2025 was the third-hottest year on record, bringing severe heat waves across Europe. Scientists warn that climate change is exacerbating the frequency and intensity of heat and dryness especially in southeastern Europe, making the region more vulnerable to health impacts and wildfires.

items.body_text:
The Israeli military began preparations for a large-scale operation in the occupied West Bank on Friday after four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers were killed in clashes there.
The military said a group of settlers entered an area of the West Bank restricted to Israeli civilians Friday for an “unauthorized and uncoordinated hike.” As the group approached the Palestinian village of Tell, clashes broke out between the settlers and residents of the village.
In the ensuing gunfire, four Palestinians and two Israeli soldiers – one of whom was also a settler – were killed, part of a surge of violence across the West Bank.
Far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the demolition of Palestinian villages in the area in response to the killings.
“The population must be evacuated for its own protection, and these villages must be cleared of terrorist infrastructure and terrorists in order to restore deterrence and security to the area,” he said Friday.
Video of the incident shows soldiers and armed Israeli settlers appearing to force Palestinians from the area, with calls for “revenge” in Hebrew heard in the background. An armed settler approaches two Palestinian men, apparently trying to use his rifle to push them away. One of the Palestinians can be seen grabbing the strap of the weapon.
Several seconds later, after the video refocuses on the incident, one of the Palestinian men is seen holding the weapon. The sound of at least a dozen shots rings out from what appear to be several different locations.
The military said the Palestinian man took the weapon from a security officer from the nearby Havat Gilad settlement. The officer was killed in the incident, it said. The military said a second soldier was also killed during the incident. It is not clear if the incident captured in the video shows the precise moment the officers were killed.
The Palestinian Ministry of Health said the four Palestinians who were killed were shot by Israeli soldiers.
Walid Zeiden, leader of the Tell village committee, said they were all members of the same family, including two brothers and two cousins. At least three others were wounded by Israeli gunfire, the health ministry added.
The UN called for “urgent action” to end the escalating violence in the West Bank amid “unabated” Israeli settler attacks against Palestinian communities.
“Israel must take immediate steps to prevent settler violence, protect Palestinian communities, and ensure that those responsible for attacks are held accountable,” said Ramiz Alakbarov, the UN’s Special Coordinator for the Middle East Peace Process, in a statement. “Palestinians must unequivocally reject violence and incitement and take immediate steps to prevent attacks against Israelis.”
The Palestinian Authority condemned the settler attacks and criticized Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz for “accelerating the establishment and legalization of colonial outposts” and reinforcing the IDF’s presence in the West Bank. It also called on the US to intervene and “compel Israel to halt its escalation and the crimes committed by Israeli colonists,” according to Palestinian news agency WAFA.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) announced that it had imposed a curfew on the Palestinian villages of Tell and Bureij, as well as the nearby Jewish settlement of Shiloh.
Despite video of the incident showing an altercation that escalated and the Israeli military acknowledging that the killing of the Israelis was not planned in advance, the IDF is treating the event as a terror attack and announced a “large-scale” operation in the area to go after “dozens of Palestinians” involved in the incident.
The IDF said it had cancelled leave for soldiers operating in the area and was preparing to send in reinforcements. Amid reports of settler attacks and raids on Palestinian villages in the area, the IDF said it was concerned by the possibility of settler violence.

items.title: El-Niño: Pouring fuel on the fire of a warming world
items.summary: Challenges exceeding the woes of energy availability might be just around the corner The post El-Niño: Pouring fuel on the fire of a warming world first appeared on Mada Masr.
items.body_text:
El-Niño: Pouring fuel on the fire of a warming world                    
                In thermal images mapping the surface temperatures of the Pacific Ocean, a thick red gash stretches, like a knife wound, out from the western coast of equatorial South America, indicating warmer than normal seas. This is El Niño, a naturally occurring climate phenomenon known to trigger weather anomalies across the globe, and its onset has been confirmed for 2026.
The secretary of the UN’s World Meteorological Organisation (WMO), Celeste Saulo, emphasized the seriousness of the situation and stressed the likelihood of regions around the world experiencing abnormal and extreme weather as a result. “In some regions it is likely we will see heavy rainfall and floods, in others drought conditions, in others increased or reduced extreme heat,” she said. UN Secretary General Antonio Guterres issued a stark warning, affirming that “El Niño conditions will pour fuel on the fire of a warming world.”
Scientists have said there is no evidence that climate change is intensifying or increasing the frequency of El Niño events. However, when coupled with higher average sea temperatures, themselves fuelled by global warming, it is likely the impacts of El Niño on global weather patterns will be amplified. The double whammy of climate change and the last El Niño event in 2023-2024 is considered to be what made 2024 the hottest year on record. At the moment, subsurface temperatures in the tropical Pacific Ocean are 6C warmer than average, fuelling concerns that the incoming El Niño could “feed on this extra heat and devastate vulnerable and unprepared communities worldwide,” according to the UN.
While there is some uncertainty about this El Niño’s projected peak strength, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Agency (NOAA), a US government environment monitoring agency, this month predicted an 81 percent chance of sea surface temperatures in the monitored region of the Pacific to exceed 2C, above the normal average for the period of October to December this year. A 2C increase is the NOAA’s threshold to categorize an El Niño event as “very strong.” A recent WMO press release also stated that forecast models are showing “remarkable agreement,” and are allowing “high confidence” in the projection that this El Niño will both develop into a strong event between now and next September, and that it will continue to strengthen throughout the autumn.
In Egypt, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbuly said, during a press conference on June 3, that temperatures are expected to reach “exceptional” levels this summer, and cited El Niño’s onset as a likely driver of the anticipated hotter weather in the country. He went on to stress the need for intensifying coordination between the central bank and the finance, petroleum and electricity ministries, with the aim of ensuring that the country’s summertime energy needs will be met.
However, the UN’s warnings hint that challenges exceeding the woes of energy availability might be just around the corner. The question is therefore raised as to what challenges the not so proverbial storm of a “very strong” El Niño is likely to pose for Egypt, and what can and should be done to help meet them.
Heatwaves
El Niño events occur every two to seven years and typically last nine to 12 months, with conditions usually forming between March and June and peaking between November and February. Impacts on global temperatures are often most significant in the second year after an El Niño event develops.
“Even with the uncertainty that always comes with seasonal forecasts, the rest of this year is unlikely to be easy,” environmental researcher Ahmed al-Adawy tells Mada Masr, explaining that even though past El Niño events have been known to reach their peak toward the end of the year of their onset, this one has already accumulated a lot of strength early on in its cycle, meaning that we are likely to see impacts earlier than we otherwise might have.

items.body_text:
What happens when a postcolonial state attempts to challenge the global concentration of advanced technology? From artificial intelligence to nuclear technology and advanced weapons, this question has once again moved to the center of global politics. Yet the struggle over who possesses advanced knowledge, who is permitted to develop it and who claims the authority to deny it to others has a much longer history.
On July 23, 1962, exactly 10 years after Egypt’s revolution, former President Gamal Abdel Nasser offered his own answer. Rockets rose over the Egyptian desert as Egypt marked the anniversary of the 1952 revolution. Nasser declared that the country had entered the missile age.
The spectacle reflected ambitions that extended well beyond the missiles themselves. Emerging from colonial rule and repeated military defeats, Egypt sought to demonstrate that it could acquire and produce advanced technologies long-monopolized by the industrialized world. For Nasser, the missile program was not simply about military power. It formed part of a broader project of technological sovereignty: the belief that political independence remained incomplete without the capacity to master modern science and industry.
The response quickly became international. Israeli intelligence launched a covert campaign against the German scientists helping build the program through intimidation, kidnappings, letter bombs and assassination attempts. West Germany struggled to balance its growing economic and diplomatic ties with the Arab world against mounting Israeli pressure and the moral and political legacies of the Second World War. Washington increasingly viewed Egypt’s ambitions through the language of regional stability, proliferation and its evolving security partnership with Israel. Even the Soviet Union, Cairo’s principal military patron, remained reluctant to see Egypt acquire capabilities beyond Moscow’s control.
At the center of these competing interests stood a group of German scientists and engineers whose expertise transformed a national development project into an international political crisis.
More than 60 years later, the questions raised by Egypt’s missile program remain remarkably familiar. Who gets to master the technologies of the future? And who claims the authority to decide?
A postcolonial quest for technological sovereignty
Egypt’s missile ambitions grew out of military defeat. The Nakba of 1948 exposed the weaknesses of Arab armies, while the 1956 Suez Crisis reinforced Egypt’s dependence on technologically superior powers. Although Nasser emerged politically strengthened from Suez, the conflict underscored that military independence remained constrained by technological dependence.
His ambitions, therefore, extended beyond acquiring better weapons. Across the postcolonial world, newly independent states invested in dams, factories, universities, laboratories and industry, not only to accelerate development, but also to reduce dependence on former colonial powers. Egypt’s missile program belonged to this broader effort. Developing an indigenous missile capability promised military advantages, but it also symbolized the belief that advanced scientific knowledge need not remain the monopoly of the industrialized world.
Yet ambition alone could not overcome structural constraints. Egypt lacked the industrial base, the scientific infrastructure and the specialized personnel needed to build advanced missile systems. Purchasing weapons abroad offered one solution, but dependence on foreign suppliers inevitably limited Egyptian autonomy. Even the Soviet Union, despite its close partnership with Cairo, remained unwilling to transfer every technology Egypt sought. Great powers, regardless of ideology, were reluctant to relinquish control over the knowledge underpinning strategic superiority.

items.title: The unregulated crocodile
items.summary: For some, the hands-off approach given the animals’ endangered status may do more harm than good The post The unregulated crocodile first appeared on Mada Masr.
items.body_text:
The unregulated crocodile                    
                
                        From tourism to illicit trade, crocodiles bring in cash. But for some, a hands-off approach given the animals’ endangered status may do more harm than good                     
                    In June, people in Hasafa village in Qalyubiya shared photos and videos on social media of a small crocodile, about a meter long, roaming through a drainage canal. A team from the Environment Ministry was dispatched to catch it, and the ministry later said the crocodile would be taken to Aswan and released into its “natural habitat in Lake Nasser.”
A few days later, another larger crocodile was spotted sliding from a muddy bank into an irrigation canal near the village of Shabramant in Aboul Nomros in Giza. Again, an Environment Ministry team located it and transferred it to one of the ministry’s facilities.
The successive sightings of Nile crocodiles so far north along the river raises questions over how they got there. Since the Aswan High Dam was completed in 1970, the species has been found almost exclusively in Lake Nasser, as changes to their natural habitat had already reduced their movement beyond the lake.
In its statement about the Hasafa crocodile, the ministry suggested that someone had thrown the animal into the canal, pointing to the illegal possession and trade of crocodiles. Ekramy al-Abassiry, the general director of the South Egypt sector of protected areas and the head of the Crocodile Management Unit at the Egyptian Environmental Affairs Agency in Aswan, offers the same explanation. Young crocodiles, he says, are taken from around Lake Nasser shortly after hatching, transported to northern governorates and sold as pets, only to be abandoned once they grow too large to handle.
The possession or transport of crocodiles — whether alive or dead — is illegal, Abassiry says. That is why many people who keep the animals avoid handing them over to the authorities once they grow too large and instead release them into public canals.
The crocodiles’ journey from Lake Nasser to northern Egypt has been accompanied by a shift in how people relate to them. Periods of coexistence were common before crocodiles were hunted for touristic and commercial purposes, despite the legal ban. Officials have repeatedly proposed regulating crocodile hunting in a way that would generate economic returns, without reaching a solution.
Before crocodiles became a commercial commodity in the second half of the 1990s, fishers around Lake Nasser hunted them for attacking fish within licensed fishing areas and damaging nets and fishing tents, Nabil Mansour, a fisher on the lake and a former candidate to lead the Aswan Fishers Syndicate tells Mada Masr.
The second half of the 1990s brought exceptional floods after years of drought, pushing Lake Nasser’s water levels to unprecedented highs. Water flowing from Sudan carried some crocodiles into the southern part of the lake, while flooding expanded the shallow waters and flood control channels that make ideal breeding grounds for crocodiles, according to officials and researchers who spoke to Al-Wafd during its coverage of the 1997 floods.
As the floods expanded the crocodiles’ habitat, encounters with people around the lake became more frequent. Between 1996 and 1998, several fatal attacks were recorded, resulting in the death of a laborer, a fisher, a mechanic at the Aswan High Dam dock and a shepherd from the Bishari and Ababda tribes. Another man survived after abandoning his camel to a crocodile. As complaints about large crocodiles mounted, the military deployed snipers around the dam’s dock during the 1998 floods to kill the animals, as they were considered a threat to workers, fishers and local residents.

items.summary: Egypt is currently drafting its second five-year National Human Rights Strategy for the 2026-2031 period to consolidate the values of democracy, citizenship, and the rule of law, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty told a European Parliament delegation on Tuesday. During the meeting, the European Parliament’s Subcommittee on Human Rights, […] The post Foreign minister outlines Egypt’s 2026-2031 national human rights strategy to European
items.body_text:
Egypt is currently drafting its second five-year National Human Rights Strategy for the 2026-2031 period to consolidate the values of democracy, citizenship, and the rule of law, Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty told a European Parliament delegation on Tuesday.
During the meeting, the European Parliament’s Subcommittee on Human Rights, headed by Member of the European Parliament Mounir Satouri, acknowledged the economic and regional challenges facing the country and praised Egypt for hosting millions of refugees and asylum seekers.
The European delegation described Egypt as a key partner for the European Union in supporting regional stability, noting the recent elevation of relations to a comprehensive and strategic partnership. The delegates called for intensified parliamentary cooperation and mutual visits to explore broader prospects for collaboration.
Abdelatty outlined the state’s efforts to upgrade its comprehensive human rights system and achieve social justice in accordance with presidential directives. He highlighted the role of the Supreme Standing Committee for Human Rights, which he chairs, pointing to recent successes on legislative, civil, and political fronts.
The minister stressed the importance of balancing civil and political rights with economic, social, and cultural rights, noting that specific attention is being directed towards women, children, youth, the elderly, and persons with disabilities.
Improving human rights conditions is an extended and cumulative process, Abdelatty said, affirming the government’s commitment to maintaining constructive dialogue with civil society and international partners, primarily the United Nations and the European Union.
Abdelatty also reviewed national programmes aimed at enhancing economic and social rights, including the “Decent Life” and “100 Million Healthy Lives” initiatives, alongside the expansion of the social protection umbrella and the development of informal settlements.
The minister noted that these advancements have been achieved despite security and economic challenges, including the threat of terrorism and the heavy burden of hosting millions of refugees, migrants, and foreign residents amid ongoing regional instability.
On the international stage, Abdelatty highlighted Egypt’s engagement with global and regional human rights systems, noting the submission and discussion of national reports before the UN Human Rights Council’s Universal Periodic Review. He added that Egypt plans to maintain an active role during its membership in the Human Rights Council in Geneva for the 2026-2028 term.
Abdelatty expressed hope that the delegation’s visit would enhance the exchange of expertise and allow European officials to closely observe the steps Egypt has taken in the human rights field.

items.body_text:
Egypt issued a statement on Tuesday strongly condemning threats by Yemen’s Houthis to impose a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia, describing the move as an irresponsible escalation that undermines regional stability.
The Egyptian Ministry of Foreign Affairs statement warned that the threats endanger the safety of maritime navigation, international trade, and vital waterways. Egypt stated the move represents a blatant violation of international law, the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, and relevant UN Security Council resolutions.
The condemnation follows an announcement by the Houthis on Monday declaring a maritime embargo against Saudi Arabia. The Houthis’ armed forces stated they were implementing the blockade “against the criminal Saudi enemy, based on the equation of ‘an eye for an eye’, effective immediately.”
The Houthis said the decision was in response to what they called an “unjust and oppressive siege” imposed on Yemen by the Saudis. A full closure of the Bab El-Mandeb Strait, the southern gateway to the Red Sea, would halt Saudi oil exports to Asia and could reduce the global oil supply by 7%.
The Saudi-led coalition in Yemen vowed to respond “firmly” to the threat against its commercial vessels, warning that the move threatens to disrupt global energy supplies beyond the Gulf.
“Such threats are a blatant violation of international law and fall under acts of maritime piracy,” the coalition said in a statement. The alliance added that it has begun implementing protection measures for its ships transiting through the Bab El-Mandeb Strait.
In its Tuesday statement, Egypt stressed its full solidarity with Saudi Arabia and all Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) countries, expressing support for all measures taken to preserve their security, stability, sovereignty, and territorial integrity. Cairo also emphasised the importance of prioritising political and diplomatic solutions to de-escalate tensions and maintain regional stability.

items.summary: Egypt will launch a sovereign-led industrial investment fund to enhance manufacturing capabilities and boost exports, alongside a separate fund targeting private sector investments in Africa, Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid announced on Tuesday. During a meeting with Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, Farid outlined the proposed investment structure for the industrial fund, which […] The post Egypt to launch sovereign industrial, African investment funds to drive economic gr
items.body_text:
Egypt will launch a sovereign-led industrial investment fund to enhance manufacturing capabilities and boost exports, alongside a separate fund targeting private sector investments in Africa, Minister of Investment and Foreign Trade Mohamed Farid announced on Tuesday.
During a meeting with Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly, Farid outlined the proposed investment structure for the industrial fund, which aims to attract long-term institutional capital. The fund will focus on priority sectors including machinery, low-voltage electric vehicle batteries, pharmaceuticals, packaging, and phosphate fertilisers, in an effort to localise industry, increase foreign exchange flows, and improve Egypt’s trade balance.
To capitalise on regional opportunities, Farid also introduced an African investment fund designed to bridge funding gaps and support the expansion of Egyptian companies on the continent. The vehicle seeks to attract domestic and international partners to build entities capable of competing in African markets and enhancing regional economic integration.
The minister also presented a forthcoming “National Initiative to Enhance Exports from Governorates,” which will operate under the prime minister’s auspices in partnership with local and international stakeholders. The programme aims to expand and diversify Egypt’s exporter base by assessing companies’ export readiness and raising awareness of foreign market requirements. Target governorates will be selected based on industrial activity volume, proximity to logistics networks, export importance, and the local regulatory environment.
To improve the accuracy of economic indicators, particularly national savings and Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), the ministry is launching a new platform to collect and analyse corporate financial statements in accordance with Company Law No. 159. Farid emphasised that the Investment Law obliges companies to disclose foreign investment data to the investment authority, noting that the ministry has contacted embassies and held workshops to ensure compliance.
Additionally, an “Investor Care” platform will soon launch as a unified official channel to receive, track, and address investor complaints. Farid noted that 69 percent of previously received complaints have already been resolved ahead of the launch, which aims to replace fragmented complaint channels with a transparent, digital system accessible online and at investor service centres.
The ministry has also activated an electronic platform for trade remedy investigations to protect Egyptian exports from protectionist measures. The system allows the investigating authority to initiate probes proactively and provides local producers, exporters, and importers with direct communication channels and an integrated database of applicable tariffs and decisions.
Finally, Farid proposed a new private-sector-managed sports investment fund designed as a commercial model to support and empower athletic talent across various sports while providing financial returns to subscribers.

items.title: Would a Consensus-Based Constituent Assembly Have Been More Effective?
items.summary: Syrians are watching closely to see whether the People’s Assembly can exercise genuine legislative and oversight authority. The post Would a Consensus-Based Constituent Assembly Have Been More Effective? first appeared on The Syrian Observer.
items.body_text:
Experiences from several post-conflict states that have successfully navigated political transitions offer important lessons for Syria’s emerging governance model. Some of the most stable transitions—such as those in South Africa and Rwanda—relied on consensus-driven constituent assemblies that brought together diverse political and social groups to shape the foundations of the new state.
Syria’s transitional authority chose a different path. Instead of adopting an inclusive constitutional assembly, key decisions about the country’s future were made largely by military faction leaders during the “Victory Conference” in early 2025.
Foremost among these decisions was the appointment of Ahmed al-Sharaa as transitional president for a five-year term. Al-Sharaa then named the National Conference Committee, which convened briefly without conducting meaningful national dialogue, before issuing a constitutional declaration and a series of sovereign decisions.
A Parliament Without Political Parties
Given the extraordinary circumstances—fourteen years of civil conflict, damaged civil registries and a vast diaspora—indirect mechanisms for forming a People’s Assembly could be justified. Yet the committees overseeing the selection of electoral bodies in each province operated under the supervision of the transitional authority’s political leadership. This approach extended to the appointment of 70 members chosen directly by the interim president, who prioritized regional, sectarian and gender balances while leaving political movements unrepresented.
The absence of structured political parties poses a significant challenge. Without formal party systems, it becomes difficult to develop coherent economic, social, cultural and political programs. Parties remain essential for managing peaceful political disagreement and preventing exclusion or violence.
The newly inaugurated People’s Assembly therefore resembles an executive-aligned body more than an independent legislature. Its ability to perform core parliamentary functions—oversight of the executive branch, accountability, and autonomous lawmaking—remains limited.
Uncertain Legislative Authority
In recent months, the transitional president has issued numerous decrees that now shape political, social and cultural life. Whether the People’s Assembly will review or amend these decrees, draft modern legislation governing political parties and civil society organizations, or pass laws recognizing international human rights standards is still unclear.
Syria has not followed the established model of a consensus-based constituent assembly to guide its political transition. Building a transparent state governed by the rule of law remains essential for reopening international engagement, attracting investment and securing reconstruction support after years of isolation and sanctions.
Awaiting Parliamentary Functionality
For now, Syrians are watching closely to see whether the People’s Assembly can exercise genuine legislative and oversight authority, hold the executive accountable for security failures, and provide citizens with assurances regarding their safety, property and rights.
The effectiveness of Syria’s transition will depend on whether its institutions evolve beyond executive dependency and begin to reflect the inclusive, consensus-driven frameworks that have underpinned successful transitions elsewhere.

items.title: Syrian Transitional Justice Court Sets July 29 for Verdict in Wassim al-Assad Case
items.summary: The court, which holds jurisdiction over transitional justice cases, concluded its third hearing on Wednesday and adjourned to review the full case file. The post Syrian Transitional Justice Court Sets July 29 for Verdict in Wassim al-Assad Case first appeared on The Syrian Observer.
items.body_text:
Syria’s Fourth Criminal Court has set July 29 as the date for issuing a verdict in the trial of Wassim al-Assad, the first case to reach judgment under the country’s transitional justice framework, according to Radeef Mustafa, Director of the Accountability Department at the National Transitional Justice Commission.
The court, which holds jurisdiction over transitional justice cases, concluded its third hearing on Wednesday and adjourned to review the full case file before delivering its ruling later this month.
In a statement to Asharq Al-Awsat, Mustafa said the proceedings had reached a pivotal stage as the court moved into closing arguments. The public prosecution presented its final legal summary, drawing on evidence, witness testimony and investigative records. The defence team then delivered its pleadings, followed by a concluding statement from the defendant.
Mustafa stressed that Syria’s transitional justice process is unfolding in accordance with legal standards designed to safeguard the rights of all parties. He noted that the court’s work is grounded in documented evidence and judicial guarantees intended to reinforce public confidence in the rule of law, judicial independence and the state’s commitment to ending impunity. He added that serious crimes are being adjudicated before specialised courts strictly through established legal procedures, ensuring fairness for victims.
Wednesday’s session, presided over by Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan, was attended by representatives of national and international human rights organisations. It also included additional testimony from witnesses called by the public prosecution.
Wassim al-Assad faces several charges, including forming and leading irregular armed groups under the direction of Brigadier General Ghiath Dalla, formerly a senior commander in the Fourth Division led by Maher al-Assad under the previous regime. He is also accused of participating in military operations targeting civilian areas in Eastern Ghouta—particularly the town of Al-Mleiha—resulting in significant civilian casualties.

Oil superpower queues up for petrol from India. Will it help Russia?
To ensure Russian petrol stations have not only queues and fistfights but something to actually sell, supplies are now being shipped across the Indian Ocean and through the Suez Canal. At least 67,000 tonnes of petrol have been shipped from India to Russia, as Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries have forced one of the world's largest oil-producing countries to turn to imports.
At the beginning of July, Russian refineries were meeting only about 65% of seasonal petrol demand. A wave of Ukrainian attacks on Russian fuel facilities reduced oil refining volumes in Russia to their lowest level in more than 21 years. In some regions, drivers queued for fuel, petrol stations imposed sales limits, and in occupied Crimea, fuel was not sold to ordinary motorists at all on certain days.
The Russian authorities expect imports, the use of reserves and the completion of refinery repairs to stabilise the market. Read on to find out who has sold Indian petrol to Russia, how much Moscow will pay for it and how much of the shortfall tanker shipments can actually cover.

items.body_text:
Ukraine is changing the future of mine action and the world should pay attention
When people think about mine action in Ukraine, they usually focus on danger. They picture contaminated farmland, damaged roads, unexploded ordnance, and the long shadow left by years of war. These images are accurate, and they reflect a very real humanitarian and operational challenge that will take years to address.
But focusing only on the danger misses an equally important reality. Ukraine is also becoming one of the most significant innovation environments for mine action in the world. What is emerging here is not just a large-scale clearance challenge, but a live testing ground for new approaches that could reshape how contamination is detected, managed, and cleared globally.
Estimates from international mine action organizations suggest that contamination may affect tens of thousands of square kilometres of territory, with some assessments indicating that up to around 30% of the country could be impacted or suspected. While such figures help communicate scale, they still do not fully capture the complexity on the ground.
A problem of historic scale
Ukraine faces one of the most extensive contamination challenges seen in decades. Following years of intense fighting across large and diverse territories, significant areas are suspected to contain landmines, unexploded shells, cluster munitions, and other explosive remnants of war. The scale is unprecedented in recent history, but the true challenge is not only about size.
A key issue is uncertainty. Not all land marked as dangerous is actually contaminated in the same way, or even contaminated at all. There is a crucial distinction between land that is potentially contaminated, land that is suspected, land that is confirmed, and land that truly requires physical clearance. These categories are often blurred in practice, yet they are essential for planning effective responses.
If all areas are treated equally, resources are spread too thin, clearance becomes slower, and recovery is delayed. The real challenge, therefore, is not only removing explosive hazards, but identifying with speed and accuracy where the real risks actually are.
Ukraine as a global turning point
Mine action has already undergone several major transformations over the past decades. It began as a largely military responsibility before evolving into a humanitarian sector. Over time, international standards improved operational safety and
coordination. Later, conflicts involving improvised explosive devices pushed the sector to adapt again, integrating new detection and disposal techniques.
Ukraine may now represent the next major shift
This is not simply because of the scale of contamination, but because the enabling conditions for innovation are unusually strong. Technology has now reached a point where it can fundamentally improve how mine action is conducted in practice. Tools such as artificial intelligence, drones, robotics, digital mapping systems, combined sensor platforms, and precision GPS are no longer theoretical. They are available, deployable, and increasingly being used in real operations.
Ukraine brings together urgency, technical talent, and operational scale. This combination creates a rare environment where existing technologies are not only being tested, but integrated in new ways under real-world pressure.
Technology can make mine action faster and safer
Traditional clearance methods are effective but slow, labour-intensive, and often expose personnel to significant risk. In many cases, deminers must physically investigate every signal detected in the ground, even when a large proportion of those signals turn out to be harmless. This makes the process both time-consuming and operationally demanding.
New technologies are beginning to change this dynamic. Drones can rapidly map large areas of terrain in high resolution, reducing the need for repeated ground surveys.

items.title: Russians attack Sumy, killing three Nova Poshta drivers – photos
items.summary: Three drivers for Nova Poshta, Ukraine's largest private postal operator, have been killed as a result of a Russian strike on a civilian facility in the city of Sumy.
items.body_text:
Russians attack Sumy, killing three Nova Poshta drivers – photos
Three drivers for Nova Poshta, Ukraine's largest private postal operator, have been killed as a result of a Russian strike on a civilian facility in the city of Sumy.
Source: Oleh Hryhorov, Head of Sumy Oblast Military Administration; State Emergency Service (SES) on Telegram
Quote from Hryhorov: "A strike by a Russian jet-powered UAV on Sumy has claimed the lives of three people – Nova Poshta drivers. The Russians deliberately hit a civilian facility where people were present and working."
Details: According to Hryhorov, the bodies of two drivers were found at the epicentre of the strike. Another man, who had been evacuated by the police in a critical condition, died on the way to hospital. The men were aged 43, 53, and 48.
A massive fire broke out at the site of the strike. Due to the threat of further attacks, rescue workers were unable to work effectively and quickly deal with the aftermath of the strike.
Nova Poshta clarified that the Russians struck the vehicle yard of the company's sorting terminal. Three drivers employed by partner carriers were killed.
"The company is in contact with the families of the deceased workers and is providing all the necessary assistance. Sadly, there are also injured drivers. Their condition is stable and their lives are not in danger. We are ensuring the affected individuals receive the support they need. Efforts to deal with the aftermath are ongoing," the company said.
The company added that customers will be compensated for the declared value of any parcels destroyed in the attack.
"Nova Poshta has activated backup logistics routes and sorting hubs to minimise any possible delivery delays. Up-to-date information on the status of parcels is available via the mobile app and on the Nova Poshta website," the company concluded.

items.title: Three civilians wounded in Chernihiv region due to enemy drone attacks
items.summary: Three people were injured as a result of Russian drone strikes in the Chernihiv region; the roof of the city’s cultural center, residential buildings, and cars were hit.
items.body_text:
Three civilians wounded in Chernihiv region due to enemy drone attacks
According to Ukrinform, Viacheslav Chaus, head of the Chernihiv Regional Military Administration, reported this on Telegram.
“Yesterday in Kulykivka, three civilians were wounded as a result of a Russian strike with Geran UAVs. The victims received the necessary medical care and were hospitalized at medical facilities in Chernihiv. Throughout the day, the enemy attacked Semenivka with FPV drones. During the day, strikes hit a private yard and cars—the vehicles were damaged, and a farm building caught fire. In the evening, a drone struck the roof of the city’s cultural center,” Chaus wrote.
In addition, in one of the villages of the Koriukivka community, Russian combat drones attacked the premises of two agricultural enterprises, causing a fire that destroyed a farm building, vehicles, equipment, and seed stocks.
“Over the past 24 hours, there were strikes on energy and communications facilities,” added the head of the Chernihiv region.
As reported by Ukrinform, more than 70,000 users in the Chernihiv region were left without power due to the Russian attack.

items.title: Three Nova Post drivers killed in Sumy due to Russian attack
items.summary: Three people were killed in Sumy as a result of yet another massive Russian attack, and fires broke out at several locations.
items.body_text:
Three Nova Post drivers killed in Sumy due to Russian attack
According to Ukrinform, the State Emergency Service reported this on Facebook.
According to the agency, civilian infrastructure and areas near residential buildings were targeted. Fires broke out at several locations—cars and non-residential buildings were ablaze.
“Rescue workers operated simultaneously at all sites to quickly extinguish the fires. They had to work under extremely difficult conditions: Due to the constant threat of renewed shelling, emergency service teams were forced to interrupt their work and take cover to save their own lives, after which they returned to extinguishing the fires,” the State Emergency Service noted.
Later, Oleh Hryhorov, head of the Sumy Regional Military Administration, clarified that the strike by a Russian jet-powered drone on Sumy killed three Nova Post drivers.
Specifically, the bodies of two victims were found at the epicenter of the strike. Another man with extremely severe injuries was evacuated from the scene by police, but he died on the way to the hospital.
“The victims were 43, 53, and 48 years old,” Hryhorov added.
According to him, the Russians deliberately struck a civilian facility where people were staying and working.
As reported by Ukrinform, an explosion was heard in Sumy on Saturday morning.
Photo: State Emergency Service

items.title: Russia’s main Black Sea oil port suspends loading operations due to drone attacks
items.summary: Sheskharis, Russia’s largest Black Sea oil port, has not been loading oil onto tankers for the past few days following attacks by Ukrainian drones in the area.
items.body_text:
Russia’s main Black Sea oil port suspends loading operations due to drone attacks
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by Bloomberg.
The Sheskharis oil terminal in Novorossiysk has not been loading oil since Tuesday morning, July 22. This is evidenced by vessel traffic data as well as satellite images confirming that the terminal has halted operations.
Although adverse weather conditions can sometimes hinder loading operations at the facility, the storm warning covering the Sheskharis area did not take effect until late Thursday evening—two days after the last loading operation was completed.
An increase in attacks by Ukrainian drones this week has already prevented tankers from loading oil from the neighboring CPC Terminal. If disruptions at Sheskharis persist, this could increase pressure on the global oil market, which is already strained due to the situation in the Middle East.
According to Bloomberg, the terminal has been shipping an average of about 650,000 barrels of oil per day this year.
The shutdown of the terminal occurred as Ukraine significantly intensified its strikes against Russian ships in the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, to force the Kremlin to end the war.
As reported by Ukrinform, on July 22, Moscow warned that navigation in its Black Sea waters had become dangerous following attacks on ships in the area.
