items.title: Giving (cautious) credit where credit is due
items.summary: In the spirit of not simply passing judgement without the intent of fairness, it must be acknowledged that a serious effort seems to have been made in response to the civil service exam cheating scandal, one that allows for a level of optimism.
items.body_text:
In the spirit of not simply passing judgement without the intent of fairness, it must be acknowledged that a serious effort seems to have been made in response to the civil service exam cheating scandal, one that allows for a level of optimism.
Just over a month ago, a bust by police and anti-corruption officials made loud the quietly known truth that there was an entire system in place to allow aspiring civil servants to cheat their way into the coveted jobs. At the time I outlined my view that the government should act with ferocity to remove those undeserving of their place in the public sector.
Not only do scandals like that of the exam cheaters occur with discouraging regularity here in Thailand, the sequence of events that follows each revelation is often maddeningly uniform.
If public outrage is strong enough, the nation can expect official promises, a committee or two being formed to “uncover the truth”, followed eventually by silence.
That tedious cycle is why this latest response deserves cautious recognition.
While the usual response is to minimise the problem and isolate responsibility to a handful of individuals, authorities this time around have shown a willingness to possibly pursue less convenient courses of action.
Unsit Sampuntharat, permanent secretary to the Ministry of Interior, said that 5,900 exam papers from the tainted round had been marked as suspect and over 3,600 of those who passed the tests face dismissal from their positions.
Eleven people, most of them civil servants, have been arrested in connection with the case, along with three said to have been the masterminds — but apparently not the biggest of the big fish — behind the operation.
These figures, while likely still far below the actual scope of the wrongdoing, are still welcome in a country where many major crimes do not result in any arrests or even tangible consequences.
Equally encouraging has been the Interior Ministry’s willingness to rethink the examinations themselves.
Just this week, a pledge was made by the office to overhaul the recruitment procedure for civil servants with the emphasis to be placed on transparency.
The goal of the revamp would be to eliminate a delay between when exams are taken and when their scores are announced publicly.
Any of these developments could still be chalked up to the usual song and dance performed by the government in the wake of a gaffe. Taken together, however, they do put up a degree of resistance to even this writer’s cynicism.
The administration of Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has even announced a broader campaign against corruption — the structurally and culturally ingrained kind that facilitated the exam cheating.
If the plan to strengthen integrity across local administrations, improve transparency and make public officials more accountable is carried out with a similar gusto to this latest sweep, it would help to differentiate it from the public relations exercises of governments past.
Ultimately, as Thailand’s history contains no shortage of ambitious anti-corruption efforts that gradually lost momentum once attention faded, any applause for these most recent moves can only be measured.
To not give credit where credit is due would nonetheless feel counterproductive to the aim of seeing real change and progress in the country.
items.normalised_title: giving cautious credit where credit is due

items.title: ‘UN stands with Syria’: Sec-gen Guterres calls for help as country rebuilds after war
items.summary: DAMASCUS, July 25 — United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged international support for Syria on Sat...
items.body_text:
DAMASCUS, July 25 — United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres urged international support for Syria on Saturday as he visited the country, which is in transition following years of war and the overthrow of longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad.
Guterres is the first UN chief to visit Syria since his predecessor Ban Ki-moon in 2009, two years before the start of Syria’s civil war which went on to kill more than half a million people before the new Islamist authorities took power in December 2024.
“I have just arrived in Damascus for a visit of solidarity. My message is clear: The UN stands with Syria at this pivotal moment and I appeal to the international community to spare no effort to support the people of Syria as well,” Guterres said on X.
State media reported that Guterres met President Ahmed al-Sharaa at the presidential palace after visiting Damascus’s Old City, with images appearing to show him at the famed Umayyad Mosque.
Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani had earlier received the UN chief and his accompanying delegation at Damascus airport.
Since Sharaa took power, the international community has urged the new Islamist authorities to build strong and effective institutions and establish a governance system that includes all components of Syria’s multi-ethnic, multi-confessional country society.
Guterres “will emphasise that the opportunity now is not only to recover from conflict, but also to lay the foundations for a future for Syria that will be more stable, more inclusive and more prosperous for all Syrians”, his spokesman Stephane Dujarric said ahead of the visit.
He will also “reaffirm the role of the United Nations is to accompany and support the Syrian people on this journey”, Dujarric added.
Civil society
Guterres is set to meet representatives of Syrian civil society and non-governmental organisations supporting women’s issues, and to visit a UN peacekeeping force that has been stationed in south Syria’s Israeli-occupied Golan Heights since 1974.
After Assad’s overthrow, Israel sent troops into the UN-patrolled buffer zone that separated Israeli and Syrian forces on the Golan, and has carried out strikes and repeated incursions deeper into Syrian territory.
Israeli officials have said they intend to keep forces in a “security zone” in southern Syria, where they seek a broader demilitarised zone.
Despite tensions between the neighbours, Israel and Syria’s new authorities have held several rounds of direct talks and have agreed to establish an intelligence-sharing mechanism, though the move has failed to halt Israeli military activity.
Syria’s war shattered the country’s infrastructure and pushed millions of people to flee internally and abroad.
Since Assad’s ousting, some 1.9 million internally displaced people and 1.7 million refugees from abroad have returned, according to the UN, while around 5.5 million people remain displaced inside the country and another six million overseas.
With many Syrians living in poverty, an estimated 15.6 million people require humanitarian assistance.
Several senior UN officials have visited Syria since Assad’s fall, including rights chief Volker Turk and UN nuclear watchdog head Rafael Grossi, while a UN Security Council delegation of ambassadors made its first-ever visit to Syria late last year.
Sharaa last year made a landmark visit to the UN where he became the first Syrian president in decades to address the body’s General Assembly. — AFP

items.title: Southern China shuts trains, schools as Typhoon Noul threatens torrential rain
items.summary: BEIJING, July 25 — Authorities have evacuated more than 20,000 people and suspended railway services in southern C...
items.body_text:
BEIJING, July 25 — Authorities have evacuated more than 20,000 people and suspended railway services in southern China as approaching Typhoon Noul threatens torrential rain and gale-force winds, according to state media.
The typhoon is forecast to make landfall in the coastal area stretching from Hong Kong to Guangdong province between Saturday evening and Sunday morning, China’s National Meteorological Center said.
It maintained an orange typhoon alert on Saturday, the second-highest level in its four-tier system, after warning that parts of Guangdong and neighbouring Fujian province would experience gales and torrential rain.
More than 20,000 people had been evacuated in Guangdong, state broadcaster CCTV said in a bulletin late Friday.
Fishing vessels operating at sea in the province had returned to ports to “shelter from the storm,” it added.
Guangdong will suspend some train services Saturday morning, with all train services in the province halted on Sunday, CCTV said.
Schools in Guangdong’s Chaozhou city were instructed to suspend on-campus activities, according to local media reports.
Extreme weather has already wreaked havoc on southern and central China this month, with 39 people killed when Typhoon Maysak triggered devastating floods in Guangxi.
Maysak also caused thunderstorms and gale-force winds that killed 11 people and injured 331 in the central province of Hubei.
Scientists warn the intensity and frequency of global extreme weather events will increase as the planet continues to heat up because of fossil fuel emissions.
China is the world’s biggest emitter of greenhouse gases, but it is also a global renewable energy powerhouse that aims to make its massive economy carbon-neutral by 2060. — AFP

items.title: Belgium detains Nato intern accused of espionage and criminal ties
items.summary: BRUSSELS, July 25 — A Canadian citizen of Chinese origin suspected of carrying out “espionage on behalf of a...
items.body_text:
BRUSSELS, July 25 — A Canadian citizen of Chinese origin suspected of carrying out “espionage on behalf of a third country” while on an internship at Nato has been arrested in Belgium, authorities said on Saturday.
The intern, who worked at the US-led defence alliance’s Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe (SHAPE) in Mons, was arrested on Thursday, the Federal Prosecutor’s Office said.
“She is suspected of spying on behalf of a third country and of being a member of a criminal organisation,” the prosecutor’s office said in a statement.
“The suspect had come to the attention of SHAPE’s security services, who reported the matter to the General Intelligence and Security Service,” the office added, without specifying the nature of the alleged spying.
After taking up the case, the prosecutor’s office entrusted the investigation to the federal judicial police in Charleroi, which carried out searches on Thursday at the suspect’s home, as well as at her workplace.
A magistrate subsequently served the suspect with an arrest warrant on Friday. — AFP

items.title: Indonesian authorities arrest former anti-corruption prosecutor after seizing US$19 million and gold
items.summary: Former anti-graft prosecutor Febrie Adriansyah has been accused of money laundering while serving as Indonesia’s top anti-corruption prosecutor. He denied wrongdoing after being questioned on Friday (Jul 24), saying he was a victim of “criminalisation”.
items.body_text:
Indonesian authorities arrest former anti-corruption prosecutor after seizing US$19 million and gold
Former anti-graft prosecutor Febrie Adriansyah has been accused of money laundering while serving as Indonesia’s top anti-corruption prosecutor. He denied wrongdoing after being questioned on Friday (Jul 24), saying he was a victim of “criminalisation”.
JAKARTA: Indonesian authorities arrested a former anti-graft prosecutor after seizing millions of dollars and more than 70 kilogrammes of gold bars from his home and other properties, an official said on Friday (Jul 24).
Southeast Asia's biggest economy has long struggled with corruption and has arrested scores of public officials in recent years.
Febrie Adriansyah stands accused of money laundering while serving as the country's top anti-corruption prosecutor, Assistant Attorney General for Oversight Rudi Margono told reporters late on Friday.
Febrie stepped down on Jul 11 after serving in the role for more than four years, following the raids on properties, including his house outside Jakarta.
Investigators seized US$19 million in various currencies and 74 kilogrammes (163 pounds) of gold bars worth millions more.
After hours of questioning, Febrie denied any wrongdoing late Friday and said he was a victim of "criminalisation" in comments to local TV.
His lawyer Febri Diansyah said his client hoped that "the legal process can proceed fairly."
The investigation against Febrie was started by police, then handed over to anti-corruption specialists in his former office.

items.title: China penalises Trip.com with US$770 million fine for online hotel-booking monopoly
items.summary: China's antitrust regulator said that Trip.com used traffic allocation, platform rules and technology to secure exclusive deals with some hotels while pushing for the lowest prices.
items.body_text:
China penalises Trip.com with US$770 million fine for online hotel-booking monopoly
China's antitrust regulator said that Trip.com used traffic allocation, platform rules and technology to secure exclusive deals with some hotels while pushing for the lowest prices.
BEIJING: China's market regulator said on Saturday (Jul 25), it had fined and confiscated a total of 5.2 billion yuan (US$770 million) from Trip.com Group for abusing its dominant position in the domestic online hotel-booking market.
Trip.com, China's largest online travel platform, used traffic-allocation mechanisms, platform rules and technical measures to strike exclusive deals with some hotels as it sought to offer the lowest prices, the regulator said.
The State Administration for Market Regulation (SAMR) confiscated 1.66 billion yuan in illegal gains and imposed a fine of 3.52 billion yuan.
Trip.com, owner of travel-booking brands Ctrip, Skyscanner and Qunar, said: "We sincerely accept and will fully comply with it, and will strictly follow the regulator's requirements to systematically implement each rectification measure, ensuring that all measures are carried out effectively."
SAMR also ordered Trip.com to refund booking deposits of 122 million yuan that it said the company had withheld from hotel operators.
The practices harmed competition and consumers by restricting hotels' ability to operate across platforms and set their own prices, the agency said in a statement on its website.
China began an antitrust investigation in Jan following complaints that Trip.com had imposed unfair terms on hotels and manipulated pricing.
The penalty comes as Beijing moves to curb unfair competition among internet platforms and excessive price competition that authorities say has hurt businesses and fuelled deflationary pressures.

items.title: Organisers raise concerns over late pullouts after Sinner, Djokovic skip Montreal event
items.body_text:
Organisers raise concerns over late pullouts after Sinner, Djokovic skip Montreal event
July 25 : The Canadian Open expressed disappointment over the withdrawals of Jannik Sinner and Novak Djokovic from next week's tournament in Montreal, saying the recurring absence of top players from ATP 1000 events had become a broader issue for the sport.
Sinner withdrew on Friday to prioritise his health nearly two weeks after retaining his Wimbledon title, while 24-times Grand Slam winner Djokovic continued to manage his workload, leaving the U.S. Open tune-up short of star power.
With Carlos Alcaraz still nursing a wrist injury that has kept him out since April, the August 1-13 tournament will again be without three of the sport's top names after Alcaraz, Sinner and Djokovic also missed last year's edition in Toronto.
"We are obviously very disappointed that Jannik and Novak won't be joining us in Montreal this year, especially after they also withdrew from last year's tournament in Toronto," said the event's tournament director, Valerie Tetreault.
"We respect their decisions and understand that, with such a demanding schedule, players' health must remain the priority.
"That said, we believe the frequency of these last-minute withdrawals in the last few years raises a broader issue for our sport. Masters 1000 events are among the flagship tournaments on the tour, and fans rightfully expect to see the world's best compete."
Tetreault added in her statement to the Canadian media that organisers were in discussions with men's governing body the ATP to ensure that the issue would receive "serious consideration" going forward.
"We firmly believe adjustments are needed in the near future to better protect the integrity of our Masters 1000 events while remaining mindful of the realities players face," she said.
The ATP did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment outside regular business hours.
CRITICISM OVER LONG SEASONS
Sinner's pullout from Montreal was particularly noteworthy given the world number one had the chance to claim all nine ATP 1000 titles in a single season, having won the first five at Indian Wells, Miami, Monte Carlo, Madrid and Rome.
The withdrawal also brought fresh focus to a packed schedule some players believe has become too demanding, with world number two Alexander Zverev among those critical of the expanded 12-day format used at seven ATP 1000 events.
More broadly, the men's and women's circuits have faced criticism due to their 11-month seasons, and both the tours came under fresh scrutiny during last year's "Asian swing" of events when extreme heat and humidity led to injuries and withdrawals.
Concerns about player availability extend beyond the ATP Tour, with top-ranked Aryna Sabalenka and Iga Swiatek among the leading women to skip this year's Dubai Championships as they balanced their schedules and recovery needs.
ATP chairman Andrea Gaudenzi defended the crowded calendar last year, saying scheduling remains the players' choice and the tour was working to set clear incentives so the right number of matches are played across the season.
The WTA told Reuters previously that athlete welfare is a top priority and it listened to views on the calendar, through the players' council and representatives on the WTA board, to improve the circuit structure in 2024 and boost compensation.
Sinner and Djokovic are expected to return to action at the Cincinnati Open next month, with defending champion Alcaraz also on the entry list, as they ramp up preparations for the year's final Grand Slam beginning in New York on August 30.

items.title: High winds could make fighting Spanish wildfires harder, officials say
items.summary: MADRID, July 25 - Winds will pick up in Spain on Saturday, with gusts of up to 60 kph (38 mph), complicating the fight against out-of-control wildfires west of Madrid, the Interior Ministry warned.
items.body_text:
High winds could make fighting Spanish wildfires harder, officials say
MADRID, July 25 - Winds will pick up in Spain on Saturday, with gusts of up to 60 kph (38 mph), complicating the fight against out-of-control wildfires west of Madrid, the Interior Ministry warned.
Two separate wildfires in the Madrid region combined on Friday and became one huge blaze, but so far they have not merged with another in Avila, in the neighbouring Castilla y Leon region.
The fires have so far forced more than 30,000 people to flee their homes in the Madrid region and more than 20,000 to be confined at home, the ministry said on Saturday, in what officials have called the region's worst fire on record.
Overnight weather conditions had helped the firefighters.
"The change in weather conditions (less wind, higher humidity, and lower temperature) has greatly benefited the fight against the forest fires, which have advanced little and decreased in intensity," the central government in Madrid said on Saturday morning.
Plumes of thick smoke could be seen in the sky west of the capital.
More than 9,000 hectares have burned in the wildfires in the Madrid region, authorities said. REUTERS

items.title: Italy defence minister offers ousted Ukraine counterpart Fedorov adviser role
items.summary: ROME, July 25 - Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said he has offered Mykhailo Fedorov, recently sacked as Ukraine's defence minister, a role as an adviser in Italy.
items.body_text:
Italy defence minister offers ousted Ukraine counterpart Fedorov adviser role
ROME, July 25 - Italian Defence Minister Guido Crosetto said he has offered Mykhailo Fedorov, recently sacked as Ukraine's defence minister, a role as an adviser in Italy.
"I called him the day after his dismissal and said: When do you want to come to Rome and work with me as an adviser?" Crosetto told Italian daily la Repubblica in an interview published on Saturday.
Asked how Fedorov had responded, Crosetto said the former minister was "moved" and saw the offer as "a demonstration of esteem and friendship".
Crosetto praised Fedorov as a driver of military innovation, saying he was "one of those people who completely rewrote the rules of the game on the battlefield". Fedorov had helped Ukraine first resist Russia's invasion and then regain the initiative by reshaping battlefield practices through new technologies, Crossetto said.
Fedorov, a 35-year-old tech-savvy reformer credited by supporters with boosting Ukraine's drone capabilities and pushing defence-sector reforms, was ousted as defence minister this month, a move that sparked rare wartime protests in Ukraine.
He was offered alternative roles by President Volodymyr Zelenskiy, but said he would not accept any other government role besides his former job. REUTERS

items.title: Romania says it shot down second drone breaching its airspace
items.summary: BUCHAREST, July 25 - Romania said on Saturday that it had shot down a second drone breaching national airspace in as many days over a sparsely populated area near the border with Ukraine.
items.body_text:
Romania says it shot down second drone breaching its airspace
BUCHAREST, July 25 - Romania said on Saturday that it had shot down a second drone breaching national airspace in as many days over a sparsely populated area near the border with Ukraine.
The first drone, which Romanian prosecutors investigating the fragments said was Russian, was shot down by the NATO state on Friday, the first time it has done so after dozens of airspace breaches.
President Nicusor Dan took to social media to say the second drone had been shot down at 8:30 a.m. (0530 GMT), 10 km (6 miles) west of Sfantu Gheorghe in the Danube Delta.
The defence ministry said the airspace breach had been spotted by radar at 8:22 a.m., and two F-16 fighter jets had been scrambled.
It did not specify the origin of Saturday's drone; prosecutors said the drone downed on Friday had been Russian.
Romania, which shares a 650-km (400-mile) land border with Ukraine, said Russian drones had breached its airspace around 30 times since Moscow began attacking Ukrainian ports across the Danube River after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
In May, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in the southeast Romanian town of Galati, near the Ukrainian border, injuring two people. It was the first time a strike had hit a densely populated area in a NATO country and caused injuries during the Ukraine war.
On Friday, General Gheorghita Vlad, the Romanian army's chief of staff, said Russian attacks on the region around the Ukrainian port of Odesa had increased ahead of the harvest season, further pressuring key energy and trade routes in the Black Sea. REUTERS

items.title: Youth account bill grants children NT$1.14 million
items.body_text:
- 
            Youth account bill grants children NT$1.14 million- By Jonathan Chin / Staff writer, with CNA
 The opposition-controlled legislature yesterday passed legislation to establish state-sponsored savings accounts aimed at boosting the nation’s birthrate by supporting childrearing and granting eligible citizens a total of at least NT$1.14 million (US$35,231) throughout their first 18 years. The bill proposed by the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and the Taiwan People’s Party (TPP) passed a third reading after a long deadlock in a vote down party lines. The law, called the Taiwan Youth Development and Future Account Act (台灣兒少成長及未來帳戶條例), is now headed for the president’s desk. Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT) and Taiwan People’s Party legislators hold signs to celebrate the passage of a bill to establish child growth and future accounts at the Legislative Yuan in Taipei yesterday.Photo: Wang Yi-sung, Taipei Times The law would create two accounts for each eligible newborn: a “Taiwan future account,” which is locked until the recipient turns 18, and an “education and development account,” with funds that could be accessed at any time. The government would open the two accounts for Taiwanese nationals who are under 18 years of age after 183 days of residency in a fixed abode on the nation’s soil, the act says. Corporations and relatives may put more money into the future account, but with significant limits on parents’ ability to access the funds. The Taiwan future account, which cannot be accessed until adulthood, could be used for the holder’s education, vocational training, professional needs, creating a start-up or housing, the law says. It would have an initial deposit of NT$60,000 and start receiving NT$30,000 annually when the account holder is six years old and end when they turn 18. The account holder, their legal guardian or close relatives may put money into the account until the account holder is 18, with no limit on the maximum annual sum. A sponsoring corporation could put up to NT$50,000 a month into an account and receive tax breaks or other incentives in exchange. The education and development account would receive an annual subsidy of NT$60,000 for account holders under seven years old, after which they would receive NT$30,000 per year until they turn 18. These accounts can be accessed any time. The Bureau of Labor Insurance will manage funds in the future accounts and guarantee returns no lower than banks’ two-year time-deposit rate, while the national treasury would cover any shortfall. The opposition’s original bill included an article that would have given corporations that sponsor Taiwan future accounts a fixed tax break. The provision was omitted in the final version, after Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) lawmakers argued that it would create a tax haven for super-rich people and exacerbate income inequality. Instead, the incentive would be determined by the government administratively. Social welfare authorities can remove control of the accounts from parents who abandon, abuse or otherwise neglect the rearing and education of their children. The agency-in-charge must return any money that had been appropriated for improper use to the account holder. The program is expected to roll out next year and cost NT$200 billion annually, according to information previously released by the government. In the Cabinet’s version, it had proposed a NT$5,000 monthly growth allowance for children until the age of 18 as part of President William Lai’s (賴清德) 18-point population strategy. The scheme would have transferred the NT$5,000 monthly subsidy to parents until the child was six, after which half would be put into a government-managed account that the child could access at 18. DPP Legislator Fan Yun (范雲) said that social experts have warned that the KMT-TPP proposal allowing additional deposits into future accounts by parents and businesses would worsen inequality through reverse redistribution. TPP caucus

items.title: USTR notices a 10% tariff on Taiwan under Section 301
items.body_text:
- 
            USTR notices a 10% tariff on Taiwan under Section 301COMPETITIVE EDGE: The 10 percent would not be stacked on MFN duties, placing Taiwan in a better position than rivals like China, academics said- Staff writer, with CNA
 The Office of the US Trade Representative’s (USTR) announcement of a 10 percent tariff on certain Taiwanese products — which was to take effect yesterday US time — is not final, but would depend on a separate investigation into alleged structural excess capacity and production in Taiwan’s manufacturing sector, Vice Premier Cheng Li-chiun (鄭麗君) said yesterday. The USTR in March announced that it had launched an investigation into excess capacity and production, as well as another probe into whether 60 economies had taken steps to ban imports of goods produced with forced labor, citing Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. The probes were intended to determine whether those US trading partners had engaged in acts, policies or practices that are unreasonable or discriminatory, and have therefore “burdened” or “restricted” US commerce, the USTR said. A US flag flies off the stern of a tour boat at the Port of Los Angeles in California on July last year.Photo: AFP According to a pre-publication version of the USTR Federal Register notice on Thursday, if the most-favored-nation (MFN) tariff on a product from Taiwan is below 10 percent, the combined MFN and Section 301 tariff would total 10 percent. Products already subject to an MFN tariff of 10 percent or more would not face an additional Section 301 duty. After the two investigations have been completed, the final tariff rate would be subject to a final determination by Washington, said Cheng, convener of the Cabinet’s Taiwan-US Economic and Trade Task Force. The USTR’s announcement on Thursday recognized Taiwan’s commitment under the Taiwan-US Agreement on Reciprocal Trade to ban imports of goods produced using forced labor, Cheng said. Taiwan and the EU were the only two trading partners among the 60 economies to receive a 10 percent tariff rate that was not added to their existing MFN duties, giving them the most favorable treatment. Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台經院) president Chang Chien-yi (張建一) said that Taiwan’s lower tariff burden could bolster the competitiveness of local traditional manufacturers, giving them an edge over rivals in Japan and China that face higher duties amid US investigations into forced labor concerns. Nonetheless, uncertainty persists over the outcome of a separate US probe into industrial overcapacity, with the findings expected by the end of this month, Chang said. The investigation could have wider implications for Taiwan’s semiconductor industry and warrants close monitoring, he said. TIER economist Liu Pei-chen (劉佩真) said that advanced-node foundries should be less affected, while mature-node foundries could face greater exposure, as concerns about excess capacity are concentrated in that segment. Chang added that Taiwan exports relatively few semiconductors directly to the US, with many shipped elsewhere for assembly into information and communications technology products. The impact could be greater if Washington imposed tariffs on finished products containing chips not manufactured in the US, he said. Chung-Hua Institution for Economic Research (中華經濟研究院) president Lien Hsien-ming (連賢明) agreed that Taiwan’s 10 percent tariff rate puts the economy in a relatively favorable position compared with Japan and South Korea, particularly for traditional manufacturing sectors. The overcapacity investigation is more likely to weigh on mature-node semiconductor production, while advanced chipmaking should remain largely unaffected, reflecting Taiwan’s critical role in the global technology supply chain, Lien said. Additional reporting by Crystal Hsu

items.title: US tariff hikes dismay and anger trading partners
items.body_text:
- 
            US tariff hikes dismay and anger trading partners- AP, BANGKOK
 US President Donald Trump’s latest set of tariff hikes yesterday drew objections the US’ trading partners, including China and Japan, with Australia slamming them as “completely unjustified.” The Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) late on Thursday announced extra tariffs of 10 to 12.5 percent on 60 economies, saying the countries had failed to adequately enforce a ban on goods made with forced labor. The new tariffs took effect just as stopgap levies Trump imposed after a stinging defeat at the Supreme Court expired at 12:01am yesterday. A customer shops for food at a supermarket in London yesterday.Photo: EPA Australian Minister for Trade and Tourism Don Farrell rejected claims linking Australia, a major exporter of beef, gold and copper, to modern slavery and raising the tariff on its exports to the US to 12.5 percent from the 10 percent level imposed after Trump’s “Liberation Day” hikes last year. “We believe that amongst all of the countries in the world Australia does take the issue of slavery, modern slavery, seriously, and will continue to do that,” Farrell told reporters in Adelaide. Australia believes the higher tariffs are “completely unjustified and we will continue to lobby the United States Trade Representative to remove all tariffs on Australian goods,” Farrell said. New Zealand Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the tariffs on his country, also subject to a 12.5 percent import duty, were “extremely disappointing,” unjustified and harmful to trade. A US investigation serving as the basis for the tariffs did not provide meaningful evidence to support allegations of forced labor. “Tariffs are not the way — they drive up costs and uncertainty for businesses,” he wrote on X. EU High Representative of Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas questioned the US’ stance in comments on Channel News Asia. “If you compare our labor laws to the ones of the United States, I mean we have, people have paid vacations, we have very good conditions, labor conditions for our employees, so it’s not really grounded,” Kallas said. Also facing a 12.5 percent tariff, Singapore’s Ministry of Trade and Industry, which reiterated its stance of not condoning the use of forced labor, said it would “continue to engage the USTR to explore options.” Japan likewise protested the 12.5 percent tariff imposed on its exports, saying Tokyo had been reassured by the Trump administration that there would be no more tariffs on top of an earlier agreement on a 10 percent US duty. “Our understanding is both sides are still committed to that,” Japanese Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara told a routine news conference. “It is regrettable that the measure imposes tariffs on the grounds of non-existence of measures banning imports of goods made by forced labor, even though Japan’s industry and trade are in line with international rules,” Kihara said. South Korea said it would maintain close communication with the US to preserve a mutual “balance of benefits.” The South Korean Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resource said the announcement eased some uncertainty over US trade policy, but noted that a Section 301 investigation into alleged South Korean excess production continues. The combined duties on South Korean exports should not exceed 15 percent, the ministry said in a statement. Thailand noted it is subject to the new 12.5 percent tariff by the US under the forced labor provision, but the measure exempts around 2,120 items, representing more than half the value of Thai goods exported to the US. items.title: China restricts exports to 14 EU entities citing national security concerns
items.summary: China banned exports of products with the potential for dual civilian and military uses to 14 European Union companies on Friday, citing national security concerns. The move comes a day after the EU imposed similar export restrictions against 51 new entities, including Chinese and Hong Kong companies, which it accused of supporting Russia’s war in […]
items.body_text:
China restricts exports to 14 EU entities citing national security concerns
“In order to safeguard national security and national interests… China has decided to place 14 EU entities including Lafert Group on its export control list,” the Chinese commerce ministry said in a statement.
China banned exports of products with the potential for dual civilian and military uses to 14 European Union companies on Friday, citing national security concerns.
The move comes a day after the EU imposed similar export restrictions against 51 new entities, including Chinese and Hong Kong companies, which it accused of supporting Russia’s war in Ukraine.
“In order to safeguard national security and national interests… China has decided to place 14 EU entities including Lafert Group on its export control list,” the Chinese commerce ministry said in a statement.
The ban, which takes effect from Friday, will “prohibit exporters from exporting dual-use items to the above-mentioned entities”, it added.
A Chinese commerce ministry spokesperson said ban was “responding to egregious actions by the EU” a day earlier.
The 14 entities include Italian electric motor producer Lafert Group, and German arms manufacturer Rheinmetall AG.
Dutch shipbuilding company IHC, which produces offshore heavy equipment, and Czech firm Tatra Trucks, which makes military vehicles, were also listed.
The ban also prohibits overseas organisations and individuals from supplying dual-use items from China to the 14 European entities.

items.title: Trump under pressure from all sides over Chinese AI surge
items.summary: US President Donald Trump is under pressure to respond to the increasing success of Chinese AI models that many companies prefer to the more powerful, but pricier, US versions from Anthropic or OpenAI. The issue came to the fore this week with the release of Kimi K3 by Moonshot, which White House officials say was […]
items.body_text:
US President Donald Trump is under pressure to respond to the increasing success of Chinese AI models that many companies prefer to the more powerful, but pricier, US versions from Anthropic or OpenAI.
The issue came to the fore this week with the release of Kimi K3 by Moonshot, which White House officials say was developed by stealing the capabilities of Anthropic’s most powerful model through a process called distillation.
The method is widely used across the industry, but US officials say Chinese firms have deployed it at scale to illicitly copy proprietary American systems.
Michael Kratsios, director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy, on Wednesday decried the practice and suggested that Moonshot had also circumvented US export curbs on powerful AI chips from Nvidia to build its products.
The Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security is formally investigating Chinese firms like Moonshot over their use of these chips, a spokesperson told The Information.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent this week threatened sanctions against China, with reports the US is also weighing a ban or curbs on foreign-made open source models that are often built through distillation.
Earlier this year Anthropic sent letters to US lawmakers warning about the practice, formally accusing Chinese firms Moonshot, DeepSeek and MiniMax of industrial-scale distillation of its Claude models.
Illicit distillation “is IP theft and industrial espionage” and “a national challenge that creates serious national security risks for the United States and democratic allies,” Sarah Heck, Anthropic’s head of public policy, said on X.
Open source, or open-weight, models cost less and use source code that programmers can customize — something that is especially appreciated by startups and companies that do not want to be beholden to models from Anthropic, OpenAI or Google that cost money and must be taken as is.
Even if just floated as an idea, the startup community has asked the White House to forgo any plan to block foreign-made open source models, saying it would just unfairly reward the US AI giants, thwart competition and stick entrepreneurs with high prices for AI.
“Lobbyists are urging Washington to treat open-model AI as a security threat. In fact, it is something more familiar: proper competition that should be welcomed,” wrote Bill Gurley, a former venture capitalist, in The Washington Post.
On Wednesday, a group of 179 startups wrote a letter to the Trump administration urging it to think twice against any outright ban or strict curbs on foreign-made models.
“Denying American startups access to models available abroad would stifle competition, entrench incumbents, and function as a tax on intelligence,” the letter from the Little Tech Association said.
‘Panic needs to stop’
Some critics of limiting open source models believe that OpenAI and Anthropic are trying to save themselves by eliminating the emergence of this rival technology.
The two AI giants are facing huge financial pressure ahead of expected IPOs in coming months, with Wall Street taking a more closer look than ever at their business performance before their expected public listings.
“The Kimi Panic needs to stop,” said David Sacks, the White House’s former chief on AI policy, who still has the president’s ear.
“President Trump’s light-touch regulatory approach is working…As long as we don’t sabotage ourselves with unnecessary rules, the US will continue to win,” he said on X.
Weighing in the debate firmly for the Chinese models was Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, whose company makes AI’s core infrastructure, whether for open source companies or US-made proprietary ones.
American companies should “absolutely” be allowed to use Chinese AI models, he said to Axios.
“These Chinese models are excellent. Open source models that are excellent should be used,” he said.

items.body_text:
Hong Kong is set for a stormy weekend with Tropical Cyclone Noul expected to make landfall between southern China’s Huizhou and Jieyang early on Sunday.
The Observatory raised the T1 standby signal at 8:40pm on Friday, with the cyclone moving west-northwest across the Luzon Strait.
“Tropical Cyclone Noul will enter within 800 kilometres of Hong Kong around this evening… The weather will still be very hot over Hong Kong during the day tomorrow (25 July). However, there will be swells,” the Observatory said on Friday.
The weather service said there were “still uncertainties [over] its distance from Hong Kong,” but it predicted heavy squally showers and thunderstorms on Sunday for the city.
Typhoon Signal 1
The No.1 signal is the “Standby” signal. It is issued when a tropical cyclone is centred within about 800 kilometres of Hong Kong and may affect the territory.
- All schools and government services remain open.
- All public transport remains in service.
- The government advice is to take the tropical cyclone into account when planning activities and be wary of potential strong winds over offshore waters.
Observatory signals currently in force
- Standby Signal, No. 1 was issued at 20:40 HKT (24 Jul 2026)
- Very Hot Weather Warning was issued at 11:45 HKT (22 Jul 2026)
Climate crisis
Tropical cyclones – which get their energy from warm ocean water – are strengthening and become ever more destructive because of warming seas. Over 90 per cent of excess heat in the atmosphere is ending up in oceans, according to NASA, as rising greenhouse gases prevent it from escaping to space.

items.body_text:
Heatwaves come and go, and while this is happening with 
increasing frequency and intensity – as this year’s record-breaking temperatures show – they slip from attention once things cool off. What does not disappear is the lasting and costly damage they do to the basic infrastructure we rely on in our daily lives.
Ultra-hot days and nights can result in the 
deaths of many people (those who cannot afford air conditioning especially) and they ignite 
forest infernos of terrifying intensity. Some of these make the news but what does not usually make headlines is the damage to roads, railways, bridges and other infrastructure.
Yet the cost is there, mounting more rapidly as each sweltering summer arrives – and it will have to be paid for by current and future generations. It is a cost that could eventually run into trillions of dollars.
Human-activity-induced climate change in general, and its manifestation in the form of stifling heat in particular, has been 
overshadowed by renewed wars in the Middle East and Ukraine, but the consequences mount with each fractional rise in summer temperatures and they cannot be ignored.
Some are taking notice. On July 15, Reuters reported on Europe’s race to protect infrastructure from heat as “railways buckle under record heat, roads melt and power grids strain”. A recently published book, Climate Change Effects on Infrastructure, examines how facilities are operating outside or at the limit of tolerance levels because they were built on assumptions that did not include climate change or extreme weather.
The problem is not, of course, confined to the European continent, and it is hardly a new one. As a report by the UN Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP) noted back in 2023, “
Infrastructure financing and climate change are the most pressing issues facing Asia and the Pacific today.”

“If they do this again, the US will hold Iran responsible, in that the Houthis are a surrogate and/or proxy of Iran, and major military punishment will be inflicted upon Iran and, of course, the Houthis, themselves,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.
The Houthis claimed a missile attack on the southern Saudi city of Jizan on Saturday, after media the group controls accused Saudi Arabia of a “dangerous escalation” and said its actions “will not go unanswered”.
Pakistan, which shares a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia, warned it would “take all necessary measures, including lawful use of force”, should its own “maritime interests” come under threat.

〔記者羅碧／台北報導〕3歲的小蘿蔔（化名）在媽媽懷孕24週又1天即出生，體重只有631公克，出生6天便因自發性腸穿孔併發失血性休克，緊急接受手術切除7公分小腸，之後又歷經慢性肺病、肺塌陷等重重考驗，住院長達6個月，返家後還必須配戴居家型呼吸器15個月。如今已健康成長，能跑能跳，今天回到馬偕兒童醫院參加「早產兒回娘家」活動，成為醫療團隊眼中最好的成績單。
馬偕兒童醫院新生兒科主任張弘洋表示，小蘿蔔因極度早產，出生後6天就發生自發性腸穿孔，併發失血性休克，醫療團隊緊急手術切除7公分小腸並設置腸造口。由於腸道尚未成熟，後續又陸續出現膽汁鬱積、骨質疏鬆等併發症，肺部也因發育不全，住院期間反覆發生肺塌陷及慢性肺疾病。
經過6個月治療後，小蘿蔔病況穩定返家，但仍須配戴居家型呼吸器持續接受呼吸支持，直到15個月後才順利脫離呼吸器。
負責手術的馬偕兒童醫院兒童一般外科資深主治醫師黃萱表示，自發性腸穿孔是超低體重早產兒少見卻相當危急的疾病，發生率約3%至5%，腸壁破洞後容易引發腹膜炎、敗血症，甚至休克。由於極低體重早產兒的腸道比烏龍麵還細，直接縫合風險極高，因此通常先以腸造口取代腸道吻合，待體重增加、腸道功能成熟後，再進行第2次手術關閉造口，以降低併發症風險。
回憶照顧過程，小蘿蔔的母親表示，孩子返家後，家裡就像一間小型加護病房，每天伴隨呼吸器及監測儀器的警示聲，必須隨時注意血氧變化、避免呼吸管脫落或阻塞，照護壓力難以言喻。由於孩子營養吸收較差，體重長期落在同齡3%邊緣，夫妻倆也配合孩子作息，在半夢半醒間餵奶，並準備蔬菜棒等原型食物，幫助孩子練習咀嚼與吞嚥。
如今3歲的小蘿蔔已就讀幼幼班，雖然仍有些挑食，卻喜歡秋葵、竹筍及玉米筍等蔬菜，也能自己拿著大雞腿大口吃飯。母親說，每一次看見孩子握住自己的手、第一次跳離地面，都讓全家感動不已。
張弘洋表示，早產兒照護不只仰賴醫療，更需要家庭長時間投入，小蘿蔔父母每天不分晴雨到加護病房陪伴，積極配合醫療團隊治療與衛教，是孩子順利跨越重重難關的重要力量。
他也提醒，孕婦若出現規律宮縮、下腹痛或出血等早產徵兆，應盡早轉診至具備高危險妊娠、新生兒加護病房及小兒外科團隊的醫院，讓新生兒出生後，立即獲得完整醫療照護，提高存活及健康成長機會。

消防局共出動消防車4輛、消防人員10名到場搶救，所幸整起火警未造成人員受傷或受困，詳細起火原因仍待調查釐清。

    雙胞胎哥哥體重過輕、糞便很淡 確診基因缺「阿拉吉歐氏症」
〔記者吳亮儀／台北報導〕一對雙胞胎中的哥哥「小宇」，出生時體重過輕，滿兩個月時「皮膚變黃、大便顏色變淡」，經台大醫院團隊檢查後，排除最危險的膽道閉鎖，確診為罕見JAG1基因缺陷所致的「阿拉吉歐氏症」。
台大醫院小兒肝膽腸胃科醫師戴季珊解釋，遺傳自媽媽的JAG1基因缺陷，在媽媽身上毫無症狀，小宇卻出現嚴重膽汁滯留。目前小宇需每日服用藥物、補充脂溶性維生素，並搭配特殊營養配方奶粉維持肝臟發育。
兒童肝膽疾病防治基金會呼籲，一旦發現嬰兒黃疸退了又復發，或大便顏色轉淡，切勿遲疑，應立即尋求小兒肝膽腸胃專科醫師協助，才能及時翻轉重症危機。
兒童肝膽疾病防治基金會今天（25日）舉辦兒童護肝保健公益記者會，基金會今年度大力推廣「兒童脂肪肝篩檢流程三步驟」，並提供實質的醫療補助，協助病童定期追蹤、重返健康。
基金會也提醒注意脂肪肝問題，兒童脂肪肝早期多半沒有明顯症狀，若未及時發現，可能逐步進展為肝臟發炎、纖維化，並增加日後罹患糖尿病及心血管疾病的風險。
基金會表示，兒童肥胖與脂肪肝涉及遺傳、飲食、生活環境及家庭等多重因素，及早篩檢、適時介入，並結合家庭與醫療團隊的支持，是守護孩子健康的關鍵。兒童肝膽疾病防治基金會現正推動「兒童脂肪肝篩檢補助」，呼籲家長主動關心孩子的肝臟健康，把握篩檢與改善的關鍵時機。

items.title: N. Korea border guard duty loses its appeal as bribes dry up
items.summary: Attitudes inside North Korea toward serving in the border guard have shifted completely. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, soldiers could collect bribes for turning a blind eye to individual smuggling. Service conditions were relatively good, and the posting was popular. Since the pandemic, tighter border controls have cut off that smuggling. The border guard is now […]
items.body_text:
Attitudes inside North Korea toward serving in the border guard have shifted completely. Before the COVID-19 pandemic, soldiers could collect bribes for turning a blind eye to individual smuggling. Service conditions were relatively good, and the posting was popular.
Since the pandemic, tighter border controls have cut off that smuggling. The border guard is now considered an undesirable posting.
A source in Ryanggang province told Daily NK on Thursday that conditions for border guard soldiers stationed in Hyesan have changed “180 degrees” compared with before the pandemic. Before, the source said, soldiers looked neat and had healthy complexions. Now, the situation is entirely different.
According to the source, the border guard was once a preferred posting across social classes. It drew children of cadres and children of ordinary people alike, and training was less intense than in regular army units. Soldiers could also build a financial foundation through bribes tied to smuggling in the border region.
The source added that before the pandemic, many soldiers saved more than 50,000 Chinese yuan, or about $7,380, during their service. They used the money to buy home appliances such as refrigerators and televisions. The goods were sent home before the soldiers were discharged.
Since the pandemic, tighter border controls have shortened the intervals between guard shifts. Workloads have increased, and soldiers can no longer collect bribes. Some are going hungry, the source said, adding that, as a result, the border guard’s popularity has fallen sharply.
Falling rations, rising hunger
Soldiers with the 25th Border Guard Brigade, stationed in Hyesan, once ate well. Before the pandemic, when individual smuggling was widespread, they had rice mixed with other grains at a ratio of seven to three. Every meal came with at least two or three side dishes.
At the time, soldiers rotated daily meal duty. The soldier on duty used money collected from smugglers to buy ingredients. He then asked local households to prepare side dishes and bring them back to the unit, according to the source.
Meals were technically the unit’s responsibility, but food supplies fell short. Soldiers made up the difference with money earned by looking the other way on smuggling, the source explained.
After the pandemic shut down individual smuggling, soldiers lost that source of income. Meals have deteriorated sharply as a result. Recently, soldiers have been eating corn with no rice mixed in. Their meals are rounded out with a few pieces of salted radish and soup that is close to salted water, the source said.
“Before the pandemic, border guard soldiers rarely felt hunger,” the source said. “Even when they were hungry, they could go to local homes to get or buy food, so they never thought about starving.”
The source added that meals are now poor. Access to local homes is strictly controlled, and soldiers cannot easily supplement their diets from outside the unit. As a result, hunger has become common.
Parents steer children elsewhere
The source said soldiers assigned to the border guard in this year’s spring conscription were almost entirely the children of workers and farmers. No children of cadres were among them, the source said. Life in the border guard is now little different from any other unit. Soldiers must ask their parents for spending money just to get by, according to the source.
Ahead of this fall’s conscription, some parents are reportedly using bribes and connections to steer their children away from the border guard. Instead, they are aiming for units known for better service conditions. In the past, parents paid bribes to get their children into the border guard. Now, the source said, some are paying to avoid it.
“Soldiers here serve almost 10 years, so parents will pay bribes to send their children somewhere with even slightly better conditions,” the source said. “Some parents are already making moves ahead of this fall’s conscription. But almost

items.title: N. Korea rice prices hit record high as exchange rate climbs
items.summary: Rice prices in North Korean markets have surged to a record high in July 2026. The spike follows a brief lull earlier this month, and it comes as the exchange rate climbs too amid expanding trade with China. According to Daily NK’s regular survey of North Korean market prices, one kilogram of rice sold for […]
items.body_text:
Rice prices in North Korean markets have surged to a record high in July 2026. The spike follows a brief lull earlier this month, and it comes as the exchange rate climbs too amid expanding trade with China.
According to Daily NK’s regular survey of North Korean market prices, one kilogram of rice sold for 40,000 North Korean won in a Pyongyang market as of July 19. That is a 28.2% increase from the survey two weeks earlier. It is also the highest price recorded since Daily NK began tracking North Korean market prices in 2009.
On the same day, one kilogram of rice in Sinuiju, North Pyongan province, sold for 40,200 won. In Hyesan, Ryanggang province, it sold for 40,600 won. Both prices set new records in their respective cities.
Corn prices have also risen sharply over the past two weeks. One kilogram of corn sold for 13,400 won in a Pyongyang market as of July 19. That is up 21.8% from the previous survey.
The same day, corn sold for 13,500 won in Sinuiju and 13,700 won in Hyesan. That marked increases of 21.6% and 21.2%, respectively, from two weeks earlier.
Corn prices had spiked to 13,900 won per kilogram in early June. They stabilized in late June as the season’s new corn reached markets, but surged again starting in mid-July.
The rise in grain prices appears to be due to a combination of factors. These include falling grain imports and a shortage of substitute crops such as new corn, wheat and barley. The rising exchange rate is also a factor.
According to multiple sources, grain imports through customs checkpoints between North Korea and China have recently declined. A source who monitors North Korea from China said grain such as rice and corn now makes up a smaller share of goods crossing into North Korea. Machinery, equipment and construction materials account for more of the trade, the source said.
The shift may not stem from direct customs restrictions on grain by North Korean or Chinese authorities. Instead, North Korean trading companies may be prioritizing imports of machinery and construction materials, which would push grain further down the list.
Dollar and yuan rates climb
Amid the trade expansion, the exchange rates for the dollar and the Chinese yuan are also rising sharply. As of July 19, the market exchange rate for the U.S. dollar in Pyongyang stood at 65,000 won, up 8.3% from two weeks earlier. Similar increases in the dollar rate were recorded in Sinuiju, Hyesan and other regions.
The won-dollar rate in Pyongyang had climbed to a record 71,800 won in May. That came amid rising expectations for expanded trade with China. The rate then fell temporarily as border controls tightened ahead of a visit to North Korea by Chinese President Xi Jinping.
Trade between the two countries has picked up gradually since a North Korea-China summit last month. That has increased demand for foreign currency needed to settle trade transactions, pushing the dollar rate back up.
The exchange rate for the Chinese yuan has risen even faster than the dollar. The yuan is commonly used to settle trade in the North Korea-China border region. As of July 19, the won-yuan market exchange rate in Sinuiju was 10,230 won, up 14.7% from two weeks earlier. A similar rise was recorded in the border city of Hyesan.
Sources inside North Korea say the exchange rate is likely to keep rising as trade with China continues to expand. A higher exchange rate would push up the cost of imports. That could add further upward pressure on prices for major imported goods, deepening the cost of living burden felt by the North Korean people.

items.title: Rising prices drive North Korean women toward prostitution
items.summary: More women in parts of North Korea are turning to prostitution to survive amid worsening economic hardship. Police have tried posing as clients to catch them in the act, but recruiters and managers screen out suspected officers before they can reach the women, and actual arrests remain rare. A source in South Hamgyong province told […]
items.body_text:
More women in parts of North Korea are turning to prostitution to survive amid worsening economic hardship. Police have tried posing as clients to catch them in the act, but recruiters and managers screen out suspected officers before they can reach the women, and actual arrests remain rare.
A source in South Hamgyong province told Daily NK on Wednesday that the number of women engaging in prostitution has grown near train stations in Hamhung and other major cities in the province. Rising prices have driven up the capital needed to start a small trading business. Women with few options are turning to prostitution instead, since it requires no upfront capital.
The province’s cost of living has pushed the capital needed for petty trade up at least fivefold compared with past years, according to the source. Wealthy North Koreans who hold foreign currency are relatively insulated from rising prices and exchange rates. Vulnerable North Korean people, who live hand to mouth, face a harder path as their trading costs have swelled just as their day-to-day income has stayed flat.
Selling rice cakes or imitation meat rice, a popular North Korean street food, once let poorer women start a business with little capital. That has changed. Rising ingredient costs and weaker buying power have made even food vending hard to profit from. Some women now sell food by day and turn to prostitution at night, the source said.
A more organized, and harder to catch, operation
In Hamhung, four or five women once worked prostitution in a given area. Now, seven or eight do, according to the source.
New arrivals once sparked conflict. Established women guarded their turf and viewed newcomers as a threat to their income, the source said. That has eased recently, as demand has grown enough to reduce competition among the women themselves.
The trade now runs through three roles: managers, recruiters who scout clients, and the women themselves. A recruiter finds a client and connects him with a manager. A waiting woman then moves to a location the manager designates.
Women typically keep 60% of what they earn. Managers take the remaining 40%, and pass a portion of that cut to recruiters, the source said.
Women once solicited clients directly on the street, but that has changed too. Showing their faces in public made them easy targets for police, so many now avoid exposure altogether.
Clients must pass through a recruiter and then a manager before reaching a woman. That structure makes it difficult for police posing as clients to catch anyone in the act.
Better organized prostitution rings
More women are entering the trade out of necessity, the source said. But the increasingly organized structure is making it harder, not easier, for police to catch them.
“Police have posed as clients and tried to make arrests, but they haven’t had much success,” the source said. “Catching someone in the act is the only way to get solid evidence. But recruiters and managers grow suspicious and turn people away the moment something feels off.”
Police often give themselves away even out of uniform, through the way they speak or carry themselves, the source said. Women who have worked in the trade for years have come to recognize officers’ faces, even without direct contact, making them harder to catch than before.
“The bigger problem,” the source added, “is that no matter how many crackdowns happen, these women have no choice but to return to the same work to survive.”

items.title: There’s more than mythology to Australia’s most hyped new rock band
items.summary: Mount Zero, the debut from Adelaide rockers Swapmeet, leads this week’s must-listens.
items.body_text:
There’s more than mythology to Australia’s most hyped new rock band
Swapmeet, Mount Zero
★★★
“Mount Zero is a place you pass but never go,” Swapmeet’s Maxwell Elphick says of the mountain that looms as the northernmost point of the Grampians.
The band would pass by the cryptically named mountain again and again while journeying from their hometown of Adelaide to Melbourne to play gigs.
These long, empty road trips have become part of the much-hyped indie rock group’s mythology – their first-ever show in Wollongong was packed full of devoted Adelaideans who’d made the trip across the border in support.
It’s appropriate, then, that their debut album stretches and turns like one of these trips. There’s the propulsive thud of single and opener I Know!, the messy dirge of Seeds and the breeziness of standout Sand, while smatterings of horns and shrieking guitars slap exclamation marks on Personal (Don’t Take it) and Halfway.
Band members Maxwell Elphick, Venus O’Broin, Jack Medlyn and Josh Doherty swap instruments and vocals throughout the album, which they pieced together in a Port Noarlunga pad that had a ping-pong table overlooking the ocean.
Despite the musical chairs, Mount Zero is a remarkably focused and even debut album, with its icy atmosphere recalling ’90s alt-rock – and a solitary drive on an empty highway. Jules LeFevre
Frost Children, Tweaker Poem
★★★★
NYC-via-Midwest sibling duo Lulu and Angel Prost have seen their star rise exponentially since last year’s Sister, their sixth album in as many years, and their production work with the likes of Kim Petras and Ninajirachi. With that increasing profile has come a major label record deal and unwanted attention of the parasocial kind.
Following an encounter with an overzealous fan (the EP’s eponymous “tweaker”), the duo fled New York and decamped to Tokyo, where – jet-lagged and sleep-deprived – they recorded this EP inspired by the entire ordeal. In songs that quote Madonna’s stalker Robert Dewey Hoskins and Rhonda Saunders’ book Whisper of Fear: the True Story of the Prosecutor Who Stalks the Stalkers, the pair scrutinise the encounter with emotional detail.
The result, somehow, isn’t dark or dour but life-affirming and warm, veering away from the brash indie sleaze they’re known for and further towards the pop aspirations and melodic melancholy that marked the best parts of Sister.
Satellites and Light Leak match their hyperpop experimentalism with the sort of chart-topping emo-EDM that poured out of dorm rooms in the mid-2010s (think the Chainsmokers, Zedd, et al.), while the sparkling synths and serrated choruses of Creep and Afterlife lie somewhere between Dance Dance Revolution and Midwest emo.
You’ll find yourself euphorically chanting “We never die, ain’t no cyanide!” over a frantic gabber beat like it’s a mantra. Robert Moran

items.body_text:
Gold Coast’s nightmare season has continued, losing to inspired Carlton by 13 points at Marvel Stadium for a ninth-straight defeat.
Trailing by 12 points at the final break, the Suns opened the last quarter with three clutch goals to reclaim the lead.
But the final term followed the script of the first three quarters – Gold Coast start strongly, before the Blues break away late in the term.
George Hewett stepped up with a huge goal, while off-season recruit Will Hayward sealed the 16.14 (110) to 15.7 (97) win for the Blues with five minutes remaining.
Premiership favourites early in the season after a superb start in March, as well as coming off a semi-final appearance last year, the Suns’ campaign has descended into chaos.
Two weeks after coach Damien Hardwick prematurely declared Gold Coast’s season over, this time he might be right.
The Suns have crashed to 7-12 and 14th on the ladder, two games away from a wildcard spot with only four rounds left.
But Carlton, who began the season at 1-8 and dealt with the departure of coach Michael Voss, have jumped to 10th with a 9-10 record to give them a serious chance of featuring in finals.
The Blues’ midfield brigade battered Gold Coast for most of the day, captain Patrick Cripps, Hewett (three goals, 24 disposals), Jagga Smith (31 touches) and Sam Walsh (31) all immense in deciding the result.
The Suns’ stars had their moments, but were never able to sustain it for long enough.
Suns captain Noah Anderson stepped up, slotting a goal of the year contender in the second term when he dodged through traffic and slipped two tackles to finish superbly.
But Anderson’s influence in the second half waned, as his opposing captain – Cripps – went to another level.
Cripps had a colossal 15 clearances from his 30 possessions to go with an important goal in the third quarter.
In his 150th game, veteran Carlton defender Nic Newman had an early finish after hurting his hamstring when wildly attempting to kick a loose ball.
AAP

items.body_text:
‘Terrifying attack’: Accused rapist allegedly ambushed woman working from home
A man accused of forcing himself into a woman’s home and threatening her with a knife before raping her on a kitchen floor has denied a string of sexual assaults in Melbourne’s outer west, including another case at a nearby school the following day.
Timothy Richards, 39, appeared in Melbourne Magistrates Court on Saturday after being charged with two counts of rape, one count of aggravated burglary and one count of threats to kill.
Police allege he knocked on the door of a house on Whitsunday Drive, in Hoppers Crossing, on Thursday while the woman was alone and working from home.
The court heard he had been living at an ex-partner’s house nearby and had approached the property 20 minutes earlier where the pair had engaged in a brief conversation.
Richards then allegedly produced a large kitchen knife and threatened to kill the 35-year-old woman before ordering her to remove her clothes as she screamed and pleaded with him to leave.
The court heard the man, who police say was wearing a hoodie and had his face covered to conceal his identity, refused and grabbed her jacket, before dragging the woman into a nearby kitchen and sexually assaulting her.
It is alleged he then pushed the woman to the ground and raped her before getting up and walking out the front door.
The woman told investigators she eventually got up and locked the door and called her husband when she realised he had left.
Sexual crimes squad detective Aiden Verdun described the alleged assault as a “terrifying attack on a vulnerable victim in the safety of her own home”.
Richards has also been accused of another alleged sexual assault on Friday, when a woman was approached outside Mossfiel Primary School, in Langridge Street, Hoppers Crossing, about 6.45am.
Police allege the woman, who was a staff member, was outside collecting bins when a man wearing a high-vis vest attempted to engage in a conversation with her before following her into a nearby classroom.
The court heard the man placed the woman in a headlock as she fought and attempted to kick him off before he allegedly raped her.
Detectives are also investigating a third incident where a 21-year-old woman was followed and grabbed at a nearby bus stop.
The woman recalled the man as being about six feet tall and of South-East Asian appearance.
Investigators are trying to establish through DNA testing if the Hoppers Crossing incidents are linked.
Richards, who denies all the allegations against him, was arrested on Friday morning.
The court heard he was on bail for three separate matters, including charges of unlawful assault, assault with a weapon, criminal damage, and possession of methamphetamine.
He appeared during a court hearing on Saturday afternoon with his shaved head down.
He will be remanded in custody and appear before a court on November 27.
Police also attended a house in nearby Branton Road in Hoppers Crossing after a resident reported a possible burglary overnight Friday.
The 39-year-old man will return to Melbourne Magistrates Court in October.

items.title: Herbicide banned in 70 countries to be pulled from sale in Australia by chemical maker
items.summary: Syngenta says it will stop selling paraquat in Australia after new regulations on chemical linked to Parkinson’s diseaseGet our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcastSyngenta, the producer of a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries and which has been linked to Parkinson’s disease, will stop selling paraquat in Australia, saying new regulations has made it “commercially unviable”.The decision to pull the product follows new restrictions on the highly poisonous chemical announced
items.body_text:
Syngenta, the producer of a herbicide banned in more than 70 countries and which has been linked to Parkinson’s disease, will stop selling paraquat in Australia, saying new regulations has made it “commercially unviable”.
The decision to pull the product follows new restrictions on the highly poisonous chemical announced by the Australian Pesticides and Veterinary Medicines Authority in June.
Paraquat has been produced by the Swiss company for decades, but has long been linked to Parkinson’s disease in users.
It is banned in more than 70 countries and has been prohibited in the European Union since 2007.
It cannot be used in domestic settings in Australia, but is still widely used in agriculture, particularly broad-acre cropping like grains, sugarcane and cotton. The APVMA assessed that the weight of evidence does not show that paraquat exposure through approved uses increases the risk of developing Parkinson’s disease.
But it did impose new restrictions to address acute exposure and risks to animals.
The company said the decision to pull the products followed a commercial review carried out in the wake of the APVMA’s rules.
Syngenta ANZ’s managing director, David Van Ryswyk, said the company will manage the phase-out of its paraquat products in strict alignment with the APVMA’s designated sell-out and use-by timelines.
“Regulatory constraints, combined with a highly complex and increasingly expensive supply chain, have made the paraquat herbicide products commercially unviable,” Van Ryswyk said.
The new restrictions on the herbicide required that backpack sprayers be phased out, mandate additional personal protective equipment for users and set a much lower maximum rate of application per hectare.
At the time of the APVMA’s decision, Syngenta said the pesticide “does not cause an unacceptable environmental impact” and that the regulation would limit its use in a significant number of crop use cases.
The company had planned to continue supplying through a third-party manufacturer, but on Friday it said the new regulations and an increasingly expensive supply chain had made the product unviable.
Generic paraquat products will still be available for local farmers.
Last month, the Melbourne neurologist Associate Prof Wes Thevathasan told the ABC that there has been “global consensus” in his field that exposure to paraquat was linked to the development of Parkinson’s disease.
“There are now multiple epidemiological studies or real-world exposure studies that have suggested that paraquat increases the risk of Parkinson’s disease by around threefold,” Thevathasan said.
Grain Producers Australia spokesperson Andrew Weidemann said Syngenta’s decision created uncertainty for local growers.
“Its withdrawal leaves some important questions about what happens next,” he said.
“Australia is a relatively small market, and decisions like this call future investment into question.
“If companies cannot see sufficient value in maintaining products here, growers risk being left with fewer choices at the same time we urgently need more tools to manage herbicide resistance.”

items.title: Lofty ambitions: can puffer jackets be made more sustainable?
items.summary: As temperatures dip, the puffer’s appeal inflates. But quality and filler are factors to consider before buying newChange by degrees offers life hacks and sustainable living tips each Saturday to help reduce your household’s carbon footprintGot a question or tip for reducing household emissions? Email us at changebydegrees@theguardian.comWhether you call it a parka, puffer or Tassie tuxedo, the insulated jacket has become a cold-weather closet staple.A 1920s version by Australian mountaineer Geo
items.body_text:
Whether you call it a parka, puffer or Tassie tuxedo, the insulated jacket has become a cold-weather closet staple.
A 1920s version by Australian mountaineer George Finch was constructed from hot air balloon fabric and eiderdown, but most modern designs are a mix of petroleum-based synthetics as well as animal and plant fibres, with varying environmental and ethical impacts.
Producing these materials, through agricultural or chemical processes, contributes 83% to the jacket’s overall carbon and water footprint, according to one life cycle study. The next largest contributor was water and energy usage during wear – with the average down jacket lasting seven years – followed by sewing and disposal. Natural fibres like down and wool also add animal welfare considerations.
But, like all clothing items, the effects are multiplied across global production and consumption systems. The market for puffers is large and growing, with more than 100m jackets made in China annually. Some brands are even branching into new territory, with demand for puppy puffers soaring.
Dr Carolina Quintero Rodriguez, a senior lecturer at RMIT University’s school of fashion and textiles, says advertising and social media are encouraging us to purchase more than we need.
“That is incentivising or creating a need in the population for not only one jacket, but you need three jackets,” she says.
A recent Adelaide University study of nearly 600 people’s clothing habits found 89% of garments are bought new, with padded jackets one of the most expensive items that people own, but rarely wear, which provides a ready supply of secondhand puffers in great condition. That’s why it’s important to choose a good quality garment, from a responsible brand, and wear it and repair it for as long as possible.
One jacket, many ingredients
Julie Boulton, a sustainable fashion consultant, says puffers usually consist of an inner and outer shell, a filler (“the stuff that makes it puff”), and notions like zips, snaps or buttons and thread.
Shells are usually made from fossil fuel-derived materials, such as nylon or polyester, sometimes blended with cotton or wool.
Jackets labelled “100% recycled” usually comprise polyesters made from plastic waste, such as water bottles or used textiles.
The padding inside often consists of duck or goose feathers (called down), wool, or a synthetic fill, Boulton says. Some brands, like Pangaia, are moving to plant-based fluff, made from wildflowers, biopolymers and aerogel.
According to the life cycle study, polyester fibre production, spinning, weaving, fabric dyeing and finishing are all high-energy consumption processes.
Polyester is a petroleum-based fibre that has issues with greenhouse gas emissions and shedding microplastics, Quintero Rodriguez says. Natural down is biodegradable and a byproduct of the meat industry, she says, but can come with risks associated with animal welfare and supply chain opacity.
Down is made by plucking the soft feathers of ducks or geese, usually after slaughter, according to the RSPCA, although a small percentage (1 to 2%) is still thought to be collected from live plucking, a practice the organisation says is a major welfare concern. Consumers are encouraged to look for the Responsible Down Standard, a voluntary certification that requires higher levels of animal welfare, traceability and prohibits live plucking.
When it comes to wool, Dr Natalie Roadknight, a senior scientific officer at the RSPCA, says the biggest welfare concern is a practice called mulesing, which involves cutting an area of skin near the tail. “It’s done while the lamb is completely conscious,” she says. “They’re able to feel the cuts”. Australia is one of the only countries where the practice is still legal, with the procedure banned in New Zealand and other countries.
Consumers can choose to avoid wool products that involve mulesing, by asking the brand directly, or looking for the ZQ Merino or the Responsible Wool Standard.

items.title: Trump vows tariffs to come for Canada over wildfire smoke that has drifted to U.S.
items.summary: U.S. President Donald Trump returned to making tariff-related threats against Canada on Friday afternoon, restating his intent to impose tariffs in retaliation for wildfire smoke drifting across the border into the United States.
items.body_text:
Trump vows tariffs to come for Canada over wildfire smoke that has drifted to U.S.
'We're going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke,' Trump tells reporters
U.S. President Donald Trump returned to making tariff-related threats against Canada on Friday afternoon, restating his intent to impose tariffs in retaliation for wildfire smoke drifting across the border into the United States.
"We're going to put a big tariff on Canada because of the smoke," Trump told reporters, when speaking in the Oval Office following an announcement relating to American nuclear energy.
Trump, who made a similar threat a week ago, did not provide any detail on how the tariffs would be implemented.
In the Oval Office, Trump also said he had "told Canada they have to do something about it," which he'd also previously stated doing.
Massive wildfires have been burning across Canada this summer, forcing communities to evacuate and spurring air quality warnings in several areas.
Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week that he had "made very clear" in recent conversations with the U.S. president that Canada was doing its utmost to control the wildfires.
- Trump vows tariffs to come for Canada over wildfire smoke that has drifted to U.S. 
- GraphicsTracking the 2026 wildfires in Canada 
Carney told CBC News that he had conveyed the size of the problem to Trump, including "the scale of the forest that Canada is blessed with — eight times the size of Texas — [and] the fact that we have effectively drought conditions that have extended from the equivalent of Texas all the way to Minnesota, to put it in American terms."
But Trump isn't the only U.S. lawmaker who has criticized Canada over the fallout from the wildfires.
A handful of members of the U.S. Congress recently wrote to Carney, accusing Canada of failing to conduct adequate forest maintenance to reduce the risk of wildfires.
However, a U.S. senator this week suggested recent statements from U.S. Republicans criticizing Canada for its wildfire management are insulting and ridiculous.
Trump administration favours use of tariffs
Laura Dawson, executive director of the Future Borders Coalition and an expert on Canada-U.S. economic relations, told CBC's Power & Politics that Trump's threat of wildfire-related tariffs against Canada is part of his penchant for "getting an impact."
"And this is definitely a line that's getting a rise out of people," Dawson said.
But she noted that tariffs needed to be based in international trade law and "there's absolutely no basis in trade law for wildfire smoke."
"So while he's getting an impact from it, I don't see even the most peculiar gymnastics by [U.S. Trade Representative] Jamieson Greer figuring out a way to translate those [threats] into cross-border trade tariffs."
Trump is an avowed fan of tariffs. His administration has favoured the use of tariffs during his second presidency — even after running into court-related setbacks in terms of how the U.S. government is able to wield them.
Earlier this week, Trump separately threatened to impose 50 per cent tariffs on billions of dollars' worth of Canadian goods effective Aug. 19.
Carney has said Ottawa will consider retaliatory measures if the federal government is unable to reach a deal with the Americans before Trump's threatened tariffs come into effect.
With files from the CBC's Andrew Kurjata and Reuters
