items.title: Why is Cair urging US Muslims to seek security from DHS?
items.summary: Why is Cair urging US Muslims to seek security from DHS? Submitted by Muneeza Rizvi on Fri, 06/26/2026 - 22:15 The grant push is only the latest in the civil rights group's decades of steering Muslims towards the institutions that surveil, entrap and deport them Police and officials brief the media after a shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego on 18 May 2026 (Carlos A Moreno/Getty Images via AFP) Off Applications for this year's round of security grants from the US Department of Homeland S
items.body_text:
Why is Cair urging US Muslims to seek security from DHS?
Applications for this year's round of security grants from the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS) close on 24 July - and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair) is urging mosques, Islamic schools and Muslim nonprofits to apply before the deadline.
Since May's mosque shooting in San Diego, which killed three people, Cair has aggressively pursued renewed Muslim community access to this source of government funding, presenting it as a means of protecting mosques from such violence.
Cair has since also encouraged Muslims to build closer ties with the police - reviving a debate over policing that reflects a growing divide within the community, between those eager to collaborate with "law enforcement" and those who view it as an arm of an unjust social order.
Cair has long walked an ambivalent line on this issue. As a self-described civil rights and advocacy nonprofit with nearly 30 chapters, it positions itself as Muslims' primary defence against "overly-broad" policing.
Yet, at the same time, it has spent decades encouraging Muslims to "build bridges" with the very police agencies whose practices it claims to challenge.
New MEE newsletter: Jerusalem Dispatch
Sign up to get the latest insights and analysis on Israel-Palestine, alongside Turkey Unpacked and other MEE newsletters
Cair's encouragement suggests that Muslims and "law enforcement" are two groups separated by unfamiliarity or misunderstanding. However, the history between them is not one of insufficient contact.
Muslims have come to know local and federal police agencies all too well through a history of hostile encounters: decades of FBI door knocks, entrapment cases, raids of Palestine encampments that local police have turned into prosecutions of Muslim students, harassment outside Zionist land sales and relentless attempts to conscript Muslims into disciplining their own communities.
Though spread unevenly, suspicion towards "law enforcement" has long existed among Muslims in the United States. Such sentiments became more visible in 2020, during the nationwide demonstrations following the police murder of George Floyd. And they have only become more pronounced since Israel's genocidal war in Palestine.
Indeed, when any meaningful resistance to US foreign policy is met with police violence, it becomes difficult to ignore the link between occupation abroad and state repression at home. Despite this growing political consciousness among Muslims, Cair remains committed to strengthening Muslim cooperation with "law enforcement".
'Best practices'
In the aftermath of the shooting at the Islamic Center of San Diego, numerous Cair branches disseminated the national office's "Best Practices for Mosque and Community Safety", a booklet aimed at leaders and everyday congregants. Its recommendations take as given that Muslims embracing "law enforcement" will protect mosques from violence and desecration.
Best practices listed in the document thus include informing local police of mosques' daily schedules, inviting police to mosques for meetings and offering police training in cultural competency.
Recommendations also extend beyond local "law enforcement". The booklet stresses: "Attempt to establish liaison with state and federal agencies in the same manner as you did with the local police. Local police may be able to facilitate this effort."
Cair's best practices appear less concerned with Muslim defence than with having Muslims project respectability
It also reminds congregations unable to afford private inspections of their security protocols that police departments can offer such assessments, as can specialists from DHS.
Most bizarre is the booklet's jumble of non-evidence-based suggestions for deterring anti-Muslim violence. For example, it urges mosques to "acknowledge good work by individual police officers" and other local officials through "complimentary letters, phone calls, tweets, social media postin

items.title: Trump says no Saudi nuclear deal if no Israel normalisation
items.summary: Trump has maintained that a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia would entail a normalisation of ties with Israel, which the Gulf kingdom has so far resisted.
items.body_text:
Breadcrumb
Trump says won't proceed with Saudi nuclear deal if no Israel normalisation
President Donald Trump on Friday said he would not go forward with a civil nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia unless the Saudis agreed to a normalisation in relations with Israel under the Abraham Accords.
The US Department of Energy said on Wednesday that Energy Secretary Chris Wright and his Saudi counterpart Prince Abdulaziz bin Salman had signed an agreement on developing the first commercial nuclear reactors in oil-rich Saudi Arabia and that it would next go to Congress for review.
Trump has been working since his first term on a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia.
Former President Joe Biden also pushed for a deal and wanted to tie it to the accords, which would normalise relations between Saudi Arabia and Israel.
But Saudi Arabia has not signed the accords because it wants an irreversible path to a Palestinian state before recognising Israel.
The accords are a major source of controversy in the Arab world and among Palestinians, and provoked a wave of anger and protests when they were first signed in 2020 with the UAE, Morocco, and Bahrain.
On Thursday, Trump suddenly publicly added the condition to the deal, saying in a post on social media that Saudi Arabia would have to join the accords.
Trump emphasised that on Friday in the Oval Office. "In order to do it, they have to be a member of the Abraham Accords," Trump told reporters. Trump said he did not talk about the accords with Wright before the Cabinet member signed the deal. "But it was always understood, and Chris knew, and Saudi Arabia knew," Trump said.
Saudi Arabia has not responded to requests for comment about the additional condition to the deal.
Trump was confident that eventually it would come together. "At some point they'll join ...and they'll do their civil, to echo it, civil nuclear," Trump said.
A deal between the US and Saudi Arabia is seen as benefiting Westinghouse, co-owned by Canadian companies Cameco and Brookfield Asset Management.
items.normalised_title: trump says no saudi nuclear deal if no israel normalisation

items.title: Saudi Arabia strikes Houthi sites in Yemen as conflict flares
items.summary: Two people have been injured by Saudi Arabia's strikes on Hodeida, the Houthis said, as conflict flares amid the backdrop of a blockade on the kingdom.
items.body_text:
Breadcrumb
Saudi Arabia strikes Houthi sites in Yemen as conflict flares
Saudi Arabia struck Houthi military targets in Hodeida on Friday with rebel media reporting two injured after the Iran-backed group announced a maritime blockade of the kingdom and hit its ships.
Saudi Arabia and the Houthis traded fire recently for the first time in years, threatening a 2022 truce that has held despite expiring.
The Saudi-led coalition said it hit Houthi sites and destroyed targets threatening commercial vessels in response to attacks on Red Sea shipping.
A Yemeni security source told AFP a naval base in Hodeida and a military camp on Kamaran island were among the targets.
The flare up followed an attack on a Saudi ship, as the rebels' maritime blockade threatened the top oil exporter's ability to supply the world following Iran's parallel blockade of the Strait of Hormuz - Riyadh's only other maritime route.
"The terrorist Houthi military targeted commercial ships in the Red Sea," Turki al-Maliki, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesman, said on X.
The coalition "carried out a decisive and strong response" targeting Houthi military sites used to threaten Red Sea shipping and that the "military response is now over", he added.
People in Hodeida heard explosions, including close to the port.
"Air strikes targeted the telecommunications building near the eastern gate of Hodeida port and the naval base at Ras al-Kathib in Hodeida," the security source said, requesting anonymity.
The Houthis' al-Masirah television said two people were injured -- a worker in the city of Hodeida and a woman on Kamaran island.
They said a telecoms building had been hit in Hodeida.
On Monday, the rebels had warned in a radio message to ships that they would target vessels "belonging to (the) Saudi enemy" that do not comply with their blockade.
Earlier this week, the Houthis claimed attacks on two Saudi ships, with Saudi Arabia confirming one of the attacks in the Red Sea.
On Friday, Saudi state media cited a transport authority official as saying "the vessel (NCC MASA), belonging to a Saudi company, was targeted while sailing in the Red Sea today... resulting in minor damage to the vessel's hull".
The ship resumed its course, the SPA added.
Red Sea access has become vital for Saudi Arabia to keep shipping oil as traffic in Hormuz is disrupted.
In April and May, all of Saudi seaborne crude exports departed from its Red Sea port of Yanbu, according to Kpler data. It represented 92 percent of all seaborne crude exports in June and 78 percent so far in July.
The Houthis have been at war with Yemen's government since 2014, in a conflict that has killed hundreds of thousands of people.

items.title: Tunisia records 900 fires in 72-hour window during intense heatwave
items.summary: Officials say most of the blazes have been extinguished but two major ones are still raging.
items.body_text:
Tunisia
At least 900 fires broke out in Tunisia over a 72-hour period, a senior official said on Friday, as the country grapples with an intense heatwave.
"These are not only forest fires but also brushland, crops, houses," said civil protection official Khalil Mechri, without offering details on the areas affected.
He said most of the blazes recorded between 20 and 22 July had been extinguished, though two major ones were still raging.
An Italian firefighting aircraft joined efforts Friday to contain the two wildfires, one of which is in the north-western region of Sakiet Sidi Youssef.
"We requested international assistance, and at the moment one Italian plane and two Algerian planes are helping to put out the fire,” said Colonel-Major of Civil Protection, Seif Eddine Dekhlaoui.
“The flames are still present. We hope that in the coming hours, the situation gets better, with wind speeds dropping and flames reducing on all fronts," he added.
The outbreak of so many blazes has coincided with exceptional heat.
Temperatures on Tuesday ranged between 40 and 49 degrees Celsius depending on the region, exceeding seasonal averages by 8 to 14 degrees.
The country is also experiencing daily planned power cuts intended to ease pressure on the grid.
The heatwave follows an especially rainy winter, and Mechri said an unusually high amount of dried-out plant cover had "contributed to the outbreak of fires".
Tunisia's director general of forests, Mohamed Noufel Ben Haha, said around 4,400 hectares of forestland burned between 1 May and 23 July, compared with 2,705 during the same period last year.
He blamed the fires mainly on negligence and criminal acts, in addition to the extreme heat.

items.title: DR Congo: More people seeking treatment for Ebola as trust grows
items.summary: Most of the 1,000 deaths from Ebola since mid-May have occurred in communities, not in treatment centres.
items.body_text:
Democratic Republic Of Congo
In the town of Bunia in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ituri province – the epicentre of the current Ebola outbreak – community trust appears to be growing.
Medical staff say more people are coming to receive treatment for the deadly haemorrhagic virus, making their care easier.
At least a dozen facilities have been attacked by ordinary people, largely due to fear, misinformation and deep mistrust of outside authorities.
Most of the 1,000 death from Ebola since mid-May have occurred in communities, not in treatment centres.
Dr Job Kkabagambe Tibasima is the deputy supervisor for the Ministry of Health at the Ebola Treatment Centre at the Evangelical Medical Centre in Bunia.
He says this is a positive shift in the relationship between communities and health service providers.
"The patient who comes to the centre receives their treatment properly and leaves without incident, and at the end, they even thank the medical team,” he says.
Despite the growing trust, the Ebola outbreak continues to outpace the response.
More than 2,500 cases have been reported so far, but as insecurity and active conflict continue to limit access to affected areas, it is estimated that the actual number could be more than twice as high.
Although contact tracing now reaches around 80 per cent of identified contacts, teams still cannot reach every community, diagnose every sick person, or deploy response teams wherever they are needed.
Priorities remain reducing transmission in Ituri by strengthening surveillance, safe and dignified burials, clinical management, and community engagement.
At the same time, there is a need to rapidly building response capacity in newly affected provinces before transmission becomes established.
The World Health Organization says this faces technical challenges, but also requires political action towards a ceasefire to improve humanitarian access and allow the urgent scale-up of operations.
It adds that people in DRC cannot face this outbreak alone. They need sustained support from the international community and, above all, they need peace.
items.normalised_title: dr congo more people seeking treatment for ebola as trust grows

items.title: World Cup: IOC says won't ask FIFA chief to explain Balogun red card controversy
items.summary: IOC member and FIFA leader Gianni Infantino will not have to explain to the Olympic body how U.S. President Donald Trump helped to stop a player’s ban at the World Cup
items.body_text:
World Cup 2026
IOC member and FIFA leader Gianni Infantino will not have to explain to the Olympic body how U.S. President Donald Trump helped to stop a player’s ban at the World Cup.
The IOC said on Friday it has no jurisdiction to investigate Infantino’s alleged lack of political neutrality.
A London-based NGO formally complained this month to the International Olympic Committee ethics commission about Infantino, including his part in ensuring United States forward Folarin Balogun did not serve a mandatory one-game ban despite being sent off in the previous game.
The IOC’s Olympic Charter cites neutrality among “fundamental principles of Olympism” for sports bodies like FIFA and its 100-plus members, which has included Infantino since 2020.
No formal investigation will be opened, the IOC said, because the complaint by rights group FairSquare did not relate to FIFA’s or Infantino’s specific relations with the Olympic body.
The complaint “refers only to (FIFA’s) decisions on its governance and its management, including its relations with government, and to (FIFA’s) implementation of the rules of its sport,” the IOC said in a statement.
“Consequently, the complaint falls outside the IOC ethics commission’s jurisdiction,” the statement said.
The ethics body does not have independent powers to start investigations and sanction officials, but can make recommendations to the IOC executive board chaired by President Kirsty Coventry. She attended the World Cup final last Sunday at East Rutherford, New Jersey.
Action has been taken against just one IOC member in the past eight years for unethical conduct: Sheikh Ahmad al-Fahad al-Sabah, a key power broker who built a reputation as the “kingmaker” of Olympic elections.

items.title: Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana lead Africa’s cocoa strategy through CIGCI
items.summary: Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana want Africa’s cocoa producers to speak with one voice. Their latest push through CIGCI aims to strengthen bargaining power and capture more value from the global cocoa trade.
items.body_text:
On 16 June 2026, in Abidjan, Presidents Alassane Ouattara and John Mahama met for a High-Level Summit on the future of their two countries’ cocoa economies. The meeting was more than symbolic. Since 2018, the two leaders have chosen to speak with one voice on cocoa. This summit marked a decisive step toward African leadership over one of the continent’s most strategic commodities.
It is worth remembering where this started. In 2019, the Living Income Differential (LID) price mechanism introduced a mandatory premium of $400 per ton. At the time, cocoa traded between $2,200 and $2,500 a ton on the London exchange. The chocolate industry was skeptical, at times openly hostile, warning the premium would destroy demand.
The 2018 Abidjan Declaration laid the groundwork for joint cocoa action. In April 2021, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana built on that foundation by establishing CIGCI.
Five years on, prices topped $10,000 a ton without manufacturers ceasing to buy – then fell sharply, exposing just how volatile the market can be. History has settled the argument: price and market must serve the farmer, not the other way round.
That principle has guided every advance CIGCI has made: coordinated farm-gate prices between the two countries, a first on the continent; national traceability systems built on the African Regional Standard for Sustainable and Traceable Cocoa (ARS-1000); and sustained scientific cooperation against the Swollen Shoot virus.
The clearest sign of CIGCI’s credibility is that other countries now want to join. In just a few years, CIGCI has become a reference point cited by the African Union and the European Union. Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana together produce 60% of the world’s cocoa. They have shown that coordinated action by producing countries can shape the sector.
Why a summit of heads of state mattered
Because this record is strong, the 16 June meeting was far more than a protocol event. It came at a critical moment: prices had fallen by more than half from their late-2024 peak, climate pressures were weighing on yields, and the chocolate industry was accelerating its shift toward products with lower cocoa content.
The two heads of state sent a message that no technical meeting could have carried out with equal force. They set clear objectives: improve farmer remuneration, and formally open CIGCI to other major African producers.
The roadmap: harmonise farm-gate prices, align marketing calendars, and strengthen coordination to gain greater leverage over multinational chocolate companies – including through increased local processing. The goal is for African cocoa-producing countries to speak with a single voice in defence of producer incomes.
Nigeria and Cameroon were invited to join. With them on board, the coalition would represent 75% of world cocoa output.
In Abidjan, presidents Ouattara and Mahama agreed to expand CIGCI to other African cocoa-producing countries. One month later, the Abuja Summit built directly on that commitment, bringing Nigeria and Cameroon into a shared regional agenda for a more competitive and sustainable African cocoa economy.
Priorities for the next phase
This renewed presidential mandate opens a second phase in CIGCI’s existence. Four priorities stand out.
First, anchor the price of cocoa to its fundamental value – production costs plus the social and environmental value the crop delivers – rather than leaving it to speculation.
Second, consolidate production through disease control, planned replanting and coordinated monitoring of climate and disease risk.
Third, assert the Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana origins more forcefully, using the ARS-1000 standard as a genuine lever of differentiation against competing origins and the rise of cocoa-free chocolate.
Fourth, capture more value without further delay. Africa grows close to 80% of the world’s cocoa yet keeps only a sliver of what it is worth. CIGCI members intend to close that gap through more local processing, higher-value products, and stronge

items.title: Africa’s minerals are not the problem. Weak governance is
items.summary: The global green transition relies heavily on Sub-Saharan Africa’s $16tn mineral bounty. Without urgent institutional reform, local communities will continue to pay the price for global decarbonisation.
items.body_text:
Every electric car, phone and wind turbine carries a piece of Africa. The continent holds nearly 30% of the world’s reserves of the minerals driving the green transition including cobalt, lithium, manganese, copper and rare earths, alongside bauxite and gold. Global revenues from just four could reach $16 trillion by 2050, enough to lift sub-Saharan Africa’s GDP by 12% or more.
Yet in the towns where these minerals are dug, the wealth remains out of reach. Communities atop the world’s most valuable deposits still lack clean water, decent roads and security. Africa’s challenge is not a lack of resources, but who governs them, who captures the benefits, and who bears the costs. Minerals do not inevitably cause conflict; weak governance turns natural wealth into grievance.
The same ground, three different outcomes
Norway offers the clearest example. When oil was found in the North Sea in the 1960s, Norway invested the revenues in a sovereign wealth fund now worth around 20 trillion Norwegian kroner (about $1.8 trillion). A strict fiscal rule limits the government to spending roughly 3% of the fund a year, so benefits are shared over time. The money will outlast the oil.
Brazil, a large democracy whose institutions have repeatedly failed communities, sits in the middle. In 2019, a tailings dam collapsed at an iron-ore mine in Brumadinho, killing 270 people; the owner, Vale, later agreed to a settlement worth about $7 billion. When oversight fails, that wealth becomes a hazard for those nearest the mines.
The Democratic Republic of Congo alone supplied about 74% of the world’s mined cobalt in 2023. Yet the communities digging it remain among the poorest. In the east, conflict is driven less by cobalt than by gold, tin, tantalum and tungsten, and by armed groups and foreign interests funding themselves through mining and extortion. Politics and history weigh heavily, but weak governance allows the wealth to leak into the wrong hands instead of building roads, clinics and schools.
The pattern repeats. In Guinea, a bauxite boom has brought protests in Boké over dust, lost farmland and broken job promises. In Mozambique’s Cabo Delgado, gas and ruby megaprojects sit alongside deep local poverty, feeding the grievances insurgents exploit. In Sudan, gold has become a currency of war, with networks tied to the Rapid Support Forces linked to gold revenues and foreign markets. Cameroon shows the same story in cold numbers: only 148 kg of gold were officially exported in 2021–2025, against 44 tonnes registered in Dubai, worth nearly 1,914 billion CFA francs (about $3.4 billion).
A positive lesson, closer to home
Africa need not look only to Norway. Botswana, once among the world’s poorest countries, used diamonds to become upper-middle-income in a single generation. It has kept peace since 1966 and channelled royalties into schools, roads and health care. It is no paradise given that inequality and youth unemployment remain high, but it proves exceptions are possible when the state is strong, honest and willing to share.
Communities on the margins
Much of the extraction is done by artisanal and small-scale miners, many of them young men and women in dangerous conditions, for a tiny share of its value. Yet they are not passive: youth movements demand fairer contracts, women organise for a voice in local decisions, and communities push for consent, safety and a fair share. Good governance means moving these voices from the margins to the centre.
The lesson is practical: publish mining contracts and disclose who really owns the companies; trace royalties to tangible benefits like a clinic, school or water project; give communities a genuine voice backed by real grievance mechanisms; formalise artisanal mining instead of criminalising the poor; and build African value addition, since raw-ore exports keep the continent at the bottom of the chain while refining at home keeps the jobs. items.title: What a Stray Dog’s Murder Tells us About Chinese Civil Society
items.summary: Wang Wang has appeared on billboards around the world – visible proof that China’s censorship does have limits.
items.body_text:
In New York’s Times Square, a giant electronic billboard recently carried five words: “Never forget. Never give up.” Similar displays appeared near the Duomo in Milan, by the Leaning Tower of Pisa, and around Taipei 101, in a wave of memorials that hit more than 200 screens worldwide.
Ordinary Chinese people paid for these displays, one small donation at a time – all to mourn a stray dog.
On June 28, in a village in Jieyang, Guangdong, five boys — all under 14 years old — tortured and killed a stray mother dog, nicknamed Wang Wang by the villagers who knew her well, and her three puppies. They dragged her by a wire around her neck, beat her with sticks, doused her in fuel and set her alight. The boys laughed while they filmed it, then uploaded the footage to social media.
Because all four were below China’s age of criminal responsibility, the official response was to send them to a “specialized school” for corrective education. There were no formal charges – and not only because of their age. China still has no national statute against animal cruelty, so there was nothing to charge the boys with.
Nearly a month later, the case is still generating thousands of comments a day across Chinese social media. The shock, anger, and grief has coalesced into a concrete demand: pass an animal cruelty law.
Internet users carried that demand offline. They crowdfunded memorial displays on commercial LED screens in shopping districts across China. A domestic cosmetics brand even ran mall ads in Shenzhen: “Resist animal cruelty; insist there be a law to rely on.”
But China’s party-state is inordinately sensitive to popular movements that call for political change, even demand seemingly as innocuous as outlawing cruelty to animals. It didn’t take long for the censorship apparatus to kick in.
In Guangzhou, screens along Beijing Road pedestrian street that had carried Wang Wang displays went dark. Staff confirmed that they had been ordered to take the memorials down. Sympathy posts were quickly deleted from Weibo. In Chengdu, a street mural painted in Wang Wang’s memory was covered over. A leaked internal notice from a district internet affairs office in Shenyang reportedly classified the campaign demanding justice for Wang Wang as a “political risk” susceptible to “malicious hype by foreign forces,” and instructed officials to inspect commercial LED screens.
The repression reach to Hong Kong, another symptom of the increasing restriction of free speech in the city. Internet users had crowdfunded a screen to display a Wang Wang memorial at the junction of Argyle and Shanghai Streets in Mong Kok. Handwritten placards appeared in Causeway Bay. Each display was shut down.
A boxing gym run by Hong Kong Muay Thai team member Leung Pak-yu hung a 5-meter banner on its external wall: a portrait of Wang Wang and her puppies beside the words “Being a minor does not mean cruelty can be lightly brushed aside.” On the morning of July 23, police officers came to the gym three times. By that afternoon, the building’s management was demanding the banner come down, citing the lease. Leung complied. Then he cut the banner apart and rehung the fragments he could – the dogs’ portrait among them – inside his own window facing the street.
Days earlier, the adoption platform Suppaw had crowdfunded HK$95,000 (roughly US$12,000) in about two hours to place Wang Wang’s image on a Hong Kong tram. They were told that while the wording passed review, the images of the dogs did not — out of concern, the tram company said, that they might “affect public sentiment.”
With Wang Wang memorials tightly policed on the mainland and in Hong Kong, overseas billboards have become the only outlet left for public anger and grief.
Hong Kongers will recognize this playbook. In 2019, they crowdfunded newspaper ads in dozens of major dailies ahead of the G20 summit, asking the international community to stand with the movement against the extradition bill.

items.title: NATO-IP4 Relations Remain Stronger Than the Last Two Summits Suggest
items.summary: Yes, the Indo-Pacific leaders were absent for the second year in a row. But that’s not because of a lack of interest in the partnership.
items.body_text:
A notable feature of the July 2026 NATO Summit in Ankara was the absence, for the second year in a row, of the four leaders of NATO’s Indo-Pacific partner countries, collectively known as the IP4: Australia, Japan, New Zealand, and South Korea. It may be tempting to see this as evidence that NATO-IP4 relations are on the downturn, but a deeper analysis does not support such a conclusion.
First, the main variable affecting the presence of the IP4 leaders was not the interest of NATO and IP4 countries in continued engagement, but the nature of the summits themselves. In addition, it is not clear that regular leader-level attendance at annual NATO summits is still a necessary driver of NATO-IP4 relations. The logic for continued cooperation between NATO and the IP4 is as strong as ever in the current geopolitical climate.
Rather than the optics of NATO-IP4 relations, the underlying substance and direction of engagement, the subleader level institutionalization of these relationships, and their application at the practical level are the critical elements for gauging commitment.
Summits Fit for Purpose
The key difference between the summits in 2022, 2023, and 2024 and the summits in 2025 and 2026 is in their structure. All three of those earlier summits involved two days of North Atlantic Council (NAC) meetings at leader level. The latter two summits had only one. Getting that attenuated timeline required cutting out the NAC leaders’ meetings with partner countries.
That change in structure primarily reflects the realities of the United States. To paraphrase the words of an allied official, NATO understands that President Donald Trump does not have the interest or attention span for a two-day summit, so the summits had to be shortened – simply as a matter of practicality and realistic expectations.
It is true that the IP4 leaders were still invited, and that most did not attend – that fact is indisputable. This decision becomes much more understandable when examined in context, however. Without an opportunity to take part in NAC discussions, the IP4 leaders were effectively invited to the rehearsal dinner, but not to the wedding itself. From the potential perspectives of busy heads of state, such an invitation simply does not carry the weight necessary to edge out competing domestic and regional priorities. It’s a nice opportunity, but – in combination with the simultaneous attendance of their defense ministers at complementary summit events for those peers – not a compelling one.
It would be a mistake, however, to equate summit representation with the current health of the partner-alliance relationships. Leader attendance at the 2022, 2023, and 2024 summits, which each featured a NAC leader-level session with IP4 partners, was critical to moving NATO-IP4 relations forward, establishing their importance publicly, and creating the momentum from the top necessary to activate national bureaucracies. Those goals have now been met substantially, making continued leader-level attendance less vital.
By 2024, all four of the partner countries had signed new Individually Tailored Partnership Program (ITPP) documents to map out their bilateral NATO relationships. They all had dedicated ambassadors to NATO at embassies in Belgium, and were engaged in specific NATO-IP4 priority areas of cooperation: Ukraine, cyber defense, disinformation, and technology.
Certainly, leader-level attention is the best driver for continued internal momentum within each country and for the further deepening of these relationships. That said, top leaders’ absence from regular summit-based intervals could be offset, to a significant extent, by the greater involvement of defense and foreign ministers and the continued visits of high-level NATO officials to the region. There is a clear effort being made at NATO to create such opportunities and by IP4 partners to respond.

items.title: The Power Behind Japan’s Takaichi Government
items.summary: Nippon Ishin has, through its alliance with Takaichi, exerted an influence on the Japanese government that far exceeds its parliamentary strength.
items.body_text:
On the day of a snap winter election – one that would ultimately end in a landslide victory for the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) – Takaichi Sanae stood alongside two men. They were not members of her own party, but rather the two leaders of Nippon Ishin no Kai: Osaka Governor Yoshimura Hirofumi and Fujita Fumitake, who leads his party’s Diet delegation. Yet Yoshimura’s stump speech hardly sounded like one delivered by the leader of a different party. In fact, it barely sounded as though Takaichi herself belonged to the LDP.
“We may not have the numbers. But we will never back down. We will not leave Takaichi-san standing alone,” Yoshimura declared. “We will not let Japan stand alone. We are determined to move Japan forward. That is the resolve with which we stand here today.”
Before they joined the ruling coalition, Nippon Ishin’s initial favorite in the October 2025 LDP leadership race was Koizumi Shinjiro, now serving as minister of defense. They shared a commitment to challenging vested interests and embraced what are often described as “neoliberal” approaches to achieving that goal. By providing the LDP with enough votes to secure a parliamentary majority – which it lacked in both houses at the time – Nippon Ishin hoped to advance a reform agenda that would have been impossible to pursue as a mid-sized opposition party alone.
Although Yoshimura never explicitly endorsed a preferred successor to Ishiba Shigeru, his description of Koizumi as a “politician who embodies the spirit of reform” and “a true reformer” left little doubt about his own – and his party’s – preferred candidate. Consequently, Takaichi’s victory came as a shock to Nippon Ishin. The party had not only expected Koizumi to prevail but also lacked close political ties to Takaichi and her inner circle.
However, the events that unfolded after Takaichi’s election opened a window that had long been thought closed. The LDP’s longtime coalition partner, Komeito, declined to form a government under her leadership, citing frustration with the LDP’s handling of the political funding scandal and doubts that the reforms Komeito sought would be implemented on its preferred timetable. As a result, the once-automatic path from LDP president to Japanese prime minister was no longer assured. The former members of the Democratic Party of Japan were seeking to reassemble. During the ensuing political deadlock, Takaichi wryly referred to herself as “the woman who may never become prime minister.”
Then came Nippon Ishin to the rescue. With the help of Takashi Endo of Nippon Ishin – who is well known for his cross-party connections and served as an intermediary between Yoshimura and Takaichi – Yoshimura came to see Takaichi as a fellow reformer, while Takaichi, in turn, came to believe that they had more in common than she had initially thought. The coalition talks gained speed, and a week after the leaders talked, there was a coalition agreement.
Since becoming prime minister, Takaichi has begun implementing key elements of the coalition agreement, many of which had already been on her own policy agenda for years and were included in her campaign platform during the February election. One example is the bill criminalizing the desecration of the Japanese flag – a measure she unsuccessfully sought to enact in both 2012 and 2021.
Likewise, the security reforms now underway reflect a longstanding agenda of LDP conservatives, including Takaichi, who had long argued that Komeito constrained their ambitions. With Nippon Ishin replacing Komeito as the LDP’s coalition partner, those constraints have largely disappeared. Although the coalition agreement was not exclusively focused on security, it was disproportionately heavy on that area, enabling the LDP’s conservative wing to pursue long-sought defense and public security reforms.

items.title: Trump’s new tariffs to cost Americans $100 billion per year
items.summary: US President Donald Trump on Thursday unveiled a new package of tariffs targeting 60 countries that account for over 99% of US imports, a move that—if upheld in court—would cost Americans an estimated US$100 billion per year in the form of higher costs. The duties, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, were announced as part of the president’s effort to maneuver around repeated court […] The post Trump’s new tariffs to cost Americans $100 billion per year appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday unveiled a new package of tariffs targeting 60 countries that account for over 99% of US imports, a move that—if upheld in court—would cost Americans an estimated US$100 billion per year in the form of higher costs.
The duties, ranging from 10% to 12.5%, were announced as part of the president’s effort to maneuver around repeated court rulings against his sweeping tariffs, including by the conservative-dominated US Supreme Court.
Jamieson Greer, the Trump administration’s top trade official, pointed to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 to justify the new tariffs, introduced with the purported goal of penalizing countries “for their failure to impose and effectively enforce a prohibition on the importation of goods produced with forced labor.”
Observers questioned the administration’s pretext. “Magically, the US tariff probe on forced labor practices is done perfectly in time to replace the generalized but expiring Section 122 tariffs,” noted Bloomberg’s Josh Wingrove, referring to the legal authority Trump cited for earlier tariffs.
Rep. Mike Levin (D-Calif.) acknowledged that “Section 301 is a law Congress passed,” but added, “What was passed in 1974 was authority to respond to specific unfair trade practices after investigation.”
“What is being done with it now is a tariff on 99% of American trade, set by Trump, with no expiration, no vote, and no ceiling,” said Levin.
“If a delegation that broad is lawful, then the tariff power in Article I means very little. The Supreme Court struck down the last version of this policy in February. The response was to avoid Congress and find a different statute and rebuild substantially the same tariffs, effective the same minute the old ones lapsed,” Levin said.
The list of countries targeted by the Section 301 tariffs includes Canada, Australia, Brazil, China, Mexico, Russia, Norway, the United Kingdom, and Vietnam.
Between the start of his second administration and January 2026, Trump’s tariffs cost American families $1,700 each on average as importers passed burdens onto consumers in the form of higher prices. The tariffs have also hammered small businesses, increased hardship for farmers, and failed to arrest the decline of American manufacturing jobs.
The Progressive Policy Institute said Thursday that the new tariffs would “likely cost Americans $100 billion a year” collectively—though the group’s trade director, Ed Gresser, said the administration’s order “looks vulnerable to challenge, and courts would have good reason to strike it down.”
“Its vague claims about forced labor abroad do not hold up,” said Gresser.
“Constitutionally, it is likely impermissible as an attempt to use a law designed for problem-solving abroad to impose a general tariff increase. And legally, Section 301 requires administrations to demonstrate ‘unreasonable acts, policies, or practices’ which impose a burden on US commerce, which this executive order fails to do.
“While making emotive claims about forced labor, it neither presents evidence that the listed countries are buying goods made with the use of forced labor, nor demonstrates that if they were, this would impose the statutorily required ‘burden on US commerce,” Gresser said.
Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-Pa.), the top Democrat on the House Budget Committee, said in a statement that “these new tariffs are more of the same: a nationwide sales tax that will make life even harder for families already struggling under the costs of Trump’s reckless war in Iran.”

items.title: Politicians vs generals: Ukraine’s long, hidden war within
items.summary: The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has dismissed the country’s commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi, after a turbulent week in which he also removed his defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov. The dismissal of the popular defense minister, who is credited by many as the brains behind Ukraine’s successful drone strategy, brought thousands onto the streets in protest. Despite the […] The post Politicians vs generals: Ukraine’s long, hidden war within appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelensky, has dismissed the country’s commander-in-chief, Oleksandr Syrskyi, after a turbulent week in which he also removed his defense minister, Mykhailo Fedorov.
The dismissal of the popular defense minister, who is credited by many as the brains behind Ukraine’s successful drone strategy, brought thousands onto the streets in protest.
Despite the clear public pressure to fire Syrskyi, Zelensky has presented his removal as part of an overall restructuring of Ukraine’s armed forces. He has appointed Mykhailo Drapatyi, commander of Ukraine’s joint forces group, to take over as commander-in-chief.
Much of the analysis of this episode has focused on personalities, presenting it as a personal conflict within Zelensky’s team.
Some saw the president’s decision to side with the unpopular Soviet-style military leadership of Syrskyi rather than the popular modernizer as illogical. But our research shows that tensions between the civilian defense minister and the military leadership are institutional.
Where such conflicts arise, the war makes it logical for the president to side with the commander-in-chief. Zelensky’s recent sacking of Syrskyi due to public pressure will not alter this dynamic.
Disagreements between civilian and military leadership are normal in any country, democratic or otherwise. There will inevitably be conflicting interests. Democratic civilian control – civilian oversight of the military with a clear chain of responsibility – helps to manage these differences on a day-to-day basis.
Nevertheless, war exacerbates normal competing interests and their political importance due to the existential threat. In Ukraine, institutional weaknesses make such conflicts more likely, and more difficult to regulate.
Zelensky’s dismissal of Fedorov highlights a pattern identified in our research of the period between 2019, when Zelensky was elected, and 2022 when Putin launched his full-scale invasion.
Democratic civilian control of the military was an official goal in line with NATO/EU requirements. Legislation was passed but its implementation was hampered by key people’s limited acceptance of the core idea – the notion that the defense minister should be a civilian.
Our interviews with participants in the defense reform process immediately prior to the 2022 full-scale invasion made it clear that the military leadership was, perhaps predictably, resisting all manifestations of civilian control.
Perhaps more surprisingly, Zelensky remained ambivalent about even its most basic requirement (a civilian defense minister). One Ukrainian defense expert captured this, telling us that Zelensky “failed to understand the logic that civilians must do the strategic policy-making.”
In line with the 2018 law adopted after Western pressure, since 2019 Zelensky has appointed five civilians as defense ministers. But the people we spoke with explained that he has always relied on the commander-in-chief for defense policymaking.
This has marginalized successive defense ministers and their attempts at reform – whether modest or radical.
It doesn’t help that the ministry has faced repeated corruption scandals relating to defense procurement. Three men who served civilian defense ministers between 2010 and 2014 (plus the chief of the general staff 2012-14) are now accused of treason for allegedly selling off military equipment without authorization.
This has made establishing the trust needed for a functioning relationship between the military and civilian leadership particularly challenging.
Institutionalized conflict
Sidelining the minister was possible because the 2018 law preserved a Soviet legacy system where both the minister and the commander-in-chief were both separately responsible to the president.

items.title: Pakistan’s only choice is active neutrality in US-Iran war
items.summary: A war is entering Pakistani homes right now. Not through headlines, but through the electricity bill, the bus fare, the price of vegetables at the local market. Wars in the Middle East rarely stay confined to the countries that start them — their consequences travel through oil pipelines, shipping lanes, financial markets, refugee routes, sectarian […] The post Pakistan’s only choice is active neutrality in US-Iran war appeared first on Asia Times.
items.body_text:
A war is entering Pakistani homes right now. Not through headlines, but through the electricity bill, the bus fare, the price of vegetables at the local market.
Wars in the Middle East rarely stay confined to the countries that start them — their consequences travel through oil pipelines, shipping lanes, financial markets, refugee routes, sectarian networks and military alliances.
For Pakistan, the escalating war between Iran and the United States isn’t a spectacle to watch from a safe distance. It’s a national emergency unfolding just beyond the western border, and across the waters the country’s economy depends on.
As of July 24, 2026, the conflict has entered an increasingly dangerous phase. American missiles have struck targets across Iran, including military and naval facilities near the Strait of Hormuz, with reports of strikes reaching further into the interior.
Iran has claimed retaliatory attacks on American positions and allied installations across the Gulf, including a strike on a base in Jordan. Meanwhile, Iran-aligned Houthi forces have hit Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea, opening a second front and threatening the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen sharply, shipping-insurance costs have climbed, and international oil prices have briefly crossed $100 a barrel.
None of this is abstract for Islamabad. Pakistan shares a long border with Iran, keeps close defense and financial ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, depends heavily on imported petroleum, hosts major Chinese investments, and still wants a working relationship with Washington.
Millions of its citizens have livelihoods tied to Gulf economies, one way or another. Few countries in the region have to hold so many competing relationships together at once.
No more comfortable ambiguity
For decades, Pakistan’s Middle East policy has rested on strategic ambiguity — staying cordial with Iran while keeping exceptionally close ties with Saudi Arabia and the UAE, cultivating China as the principal strategic partner while periodically rebuilding relations with Washington.
That balancing act was never easy, but it held up reasonably well as long as regional rivalries stayed short of open war.
It gets much harder when missiles are crossing borders, American installations in Gulf countries are being hit and the shipping lanes Pakistan relies on are under military pressure. Restraint and neutrality, in the old vocabulary, aren’t enough anymore.
What the country needs now is a clearly stated doctrine of active neutrality — which doesn’t mean indifference, and doesn’t mean pretending every party in this war carries equal weight.
It means refusing to take part in offensive operations, while actively protecting Pakistani territory, shipping, citizens and economic interests, and using every diplomatic channel available to slow the escalation down.
The Foreign Office has repeatedly called on all sides to show restraint and has said sustained dialogue is the only real path forward. That’s the right instinct, and it should stay the foundation of policy. But it needs to be backed by something visible.
Pakistan should state plainly that its territory, airspace, ports and intelligence infrastructure will not be used to launch attacks on Iran — and just as plainly, that any attack on Pakistani territory, vessels or civilians will be treated as a violation of sovereignty.
Defend the country, yes. But don’t let it become a battlefield, a barracks, or a launching pad for somebody else’s war.
Wartime decisions have a habit of hiding behind the language of national security. That would be a mistake here. Any Pakistani military commitment beyond straightforward territorial defense ought to go through parliamentary debate and a public explanation.
The government should brief political parties on existing defense commitments, on how Pakistani facilities are being used, on the risks at the border and on what escalation would cost economically.

items.title: Fiscal Karim Khan es destituido de la CPI por presunta conducta sexual indebida

items.title: Football chief comments on South Africa’s immigration crackdown
items.summary: The head of African football says South Africa cannot support illegal migration amid growing protests over undocumented foreign nationals Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
Football chief comments on South Africa’s immigration crackdown
Confederation of African Football (CAF) President Patrice Motsepe has backed tougher action against illegal immigration in South Africa, saying concerns about unemployment and businesses hiring foreign workers willing to accept lower wages are legitimate. Motsepe made the remarks during the CAF press conference in Johannesburg on Wednesday.
“(The) concern about our people not getting jobs is a legitimate concern. And we’ve got a duty to do that. And of course there’s also an equally legitimate concern when some of our businesses don’t employ South Africans but employ people from outside the continent because they are prepared to accept low wages. It’s wrong,” he said.
Motsepe noted that South Africa needed to address illegal migration while promoting cooperation among African countries. “We have to say we support the cooperation, the working together of Africans of the continent. We will not tolerate, we cannot support illegality. We cannot support illegal migration,” he added.
Motsepe also stressed that African countries needed to work together to create economic opportunities and reduce the pressure that drives migration. “If you don’t create jobs in Limpopo, you don’t create jobs in KwaZulu-Natal, you don’t create jobs in the Eastern Cape, people will leave the rural areas and come to the cities because they need jobs. So we need to work together to try and create jobs in the countries, in our neighbouring countries,” he said.
The CAF head's comments come amid growing protests over illegal immigration, with some groups calling for undocumented foreign nationals to leave South Africa. Hundreds of migrants continue to arrive at the Musina Repatriation Centre in Limpopo as authorities continue deportations and voluntary repatriations.
Some foreign nationals have returned to countries including Mozambique and Malawi, while others have reportedly been left stranded without the means to return home. The voluntary repatriation programme has also drawn criticism from some quarters across Africa, including Ghana.
Earlier this month, Presidency spokesperson Vincent Magwenya said the government was concerned about what it described as a campaign aimed at isolating South Africa from the continent following tensions over anti-illegal immigration protests. Magwenya said the government had observed efforts to portray South Africa as a country hostile to foreign nationals, despite official statements condemning vigilantism and reaffirming the state’s responsibility to enforce immigration laws.
“This is despite numerous official government communications condemning acts of vigilantism against foreign nationals, asserting the state’s primary role in enforcing immigration laws, and reaffirming its commitment to the supremacy of the Constitution,” he said.
Magwenya noted the government was particularly concerned about the spread of misinformation by a diplomatic representative. He later confirmed that he was referring to Ghana’s High Commissioner.
“Recent evidence shows that this false campaign, concerning as it is, is faltering. South Africa is not isolated,” Magwenya said, adding that South Africa remained committed to engagement with African countries and the international community.

items.title: South African court rules on Ramaphosa impeachment hearings
items.summary: A South African court has temporarily halted public impeachment hearings against President Cyril Ramaphosa over alleged financial misconduct Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
South African court rules on Ramaphosa impeachment hearings
A South African court has temporarily halted public impeachment hearings against President Cyril Ramaphosa over a long-running scandal involving $580,000 stolen from his private game farm.
The Western Cape High Court ruled on Friday that Parliament’s Section 89 impeachment committee could not proceed with public hearings until it decides Ramaphosa’s separate application to overturn the report underpinning the inquiry.
The 2-1 majority ruling does not prevent the committee from continuing preparatory work. Its chairman, Makashule Gana, said members would study the judgment to determine “which aspect of the work we can proceed with.”
Ramaphosa’s office welcomed the decision, saying the president “reaffirms his respect of judicial independence and separation of powers” and would continue to cooperate with accountability processes.
The case stems from the Phala Phala scandal, a 2020 burglary at Ramaphosa’s private game farm in Limpopo, where Ramaphosa claims that around $580,000 in foreign currency hidden in a couch was stolen. However, former spy boss Arthur Fraser alleged that the sum was in fact $4 million. Ramaphosa has denied any wrongdoing, saying the money came from a legitimate sale of buffaloes.
An independent parliamentary panel concluded in 2022 that there was prima facie evidence that Ramaphosa may have violated the law and his oath of office. The National Assembly rejected the report that year, when the African National Congress (ANC) held a parliamentary majority.
However, the Constitutional Court overturned that decision in May, ruling that Parliament acted irrationally, and ordered the report to be referred to an impeachment committee for review. Ramaphosa subsequently asked the High Court to set the report aside, arguing that it relied on hearsay and failed to distinguish prima facie from sufficient evidence. That challenge is expected to be heard in September.
Opposition parties have criticized the ruling, with African Transformation Movement leader Vuyo Zungula describing it as “nothing else but a delay,” South African broadcaster eNCA reported. The uMkhonto weSizwe Party also expressed disappointment, while Democratic Alliance MP Glynnis Breytenbach said the outcome “was to be expected” and would not prevent the impeachment committee from continuing its preparatory work.
If the committee ultimately finds grounds for impeachment, Ramaphosa’s removal would require support from at least two-thirds (267) of the 400-member National Assembly. His ANC lost its majority in 2024 but still holds 159 seats, enough to block impeachment if its lawmakers remain united. The party now governs through a ten-party Government of National Unity that includes the Democratic Alliance, the second-largest party, and several smaller parties.

items.title: British Army faces Kenya setback amid row over troops’ crimes
items.summary: The British Ministry of Defence has said it was forced to cancel a major army exercise in Kenya after failing to obtain the required license Read Full Article at RT.com
items.body_text:
British Army faces Kenya setback amid row over troops’ crimes
The UK has canceled a major army exercise in Kenya after the two countries failed to resolve a dispute over Nairobi’s powers to prosecute British soldiers accused of committing crimes in the East African nation.
The planned Exercise Haraka Storm, involving the 1st Battalion and The Duke of Lancaster’s Regiment, was reportedly scheduled to begin in September in central Kenya’s Laikipia County. It will instead be held outside Kenya, the British Ministry of Defence said on Thursday, according to The Guardian. Kenya’s Standard newspaper reported that the training would be moved to neighboring Tanzania. 
“It is with regret that the necessary licences required to allow training to take place in Laikipia later this year have not been forthcoming,” a Ministry of Defence spokesperson said.
The African state hosts a permanent British Army training support unit, known as BATUK, in Nanyuki, about 200km (125 miles) north of the capital, Nairobi. British troops have trained there since Kenya’s independence in 1963, conducting infantry exercises, as well as engineering and medical deployments under a bilateral defense cooperation agreement.
Kenyan lawmakers have, however, withheld approval for a renewed bilateral defense agreement amid demands for greater jurisdiction over serious offenses committed by British troops. Funding for BATUK is also reportedly under negotiation.
The unit has faced widespread allegations of misconduct, including murder, rape, and environmental pollution. A two-year Kenyan parliamentary investigation report released last December accused British soldiers of murder, sexual assault, torture, and forcibly evicting residents near Nanyuki. It also documented claims involving civilian deaths and injuries from unexploded ordnance, pollution, toxic-waste disposal, and damage to wildlife habitats.
Former serviceman Robert Purkiss has been charged in Kenya with the 2012 murder of 21-year-old Agnes Wanjiru. He is contesting extradition from Britain. Wanjiru’s body was found in a septic tank near a Nanyuki hotel after she was last seen with British troops. Purkiss denies the charge.
Last year, Britain agreed to pay £2.9 million ($3.9 million) to more than 7,700 Kenyans and an environmental group over a 2021 wildfire accidentally started by British troops. The blaze destroyed more than 12,000 acres of the Lolldaiga Hills and reportedly caused one death.
The Ministry of Defence said it remained committed to its defense partnership with Kenya and would continue talks aimed at resuming training.
Nelson Koech, chairman of the Kenyan parliament’s defense committee, said Nairobi is seeking stronger accountability measures, greater protection for local communities, and implementation of the BATUK inquiry’s recommendations.
The two governments are “actively engaging to address these outstanding issues,” The Guardian quoted Koech as saying.

items.title: Pope to Church in Asia: United in charity build bridges throughout the continent
items.summary: Pope Leo invites Bishops gathered in Jakarta, Indonesia, for the 12th Plenary Assembly of the Federation of Asian Bishops' Conferences to be an ever greater sign of God's presence in their various countries, as they discuss the important issues affecting the life and future of the Catholic Church in Asia. Read all
items.body_text:
Pope to Church in Asia: United in charity build bridges throughout the continent
By Deborah Castellano Lubov
"As you gather to discuss the important issues affecting the life and future of the Catholic Church in Asia, I assure you of my spiritual closeness, praying that the Holy Spirit will inspire and guide your time together."
Pope Leo XIV expressed this in the video message he sent on Saturday to the Bishops and members gathered in Jakarta, Indonesia, for the 12th Plenary Assembly of the Federation of Asian Bishops' Conferences (FABC), taking place from July 20 to 26.
Jesus is the source of our communion
In the message, the Pope recalled that the theme chosen for their Assembly comes from Jesus telling Nathanael: âYou will see greater thingsâ (Jn 1:50), noting, that "in calling Philip and Nathanael to follow Him and become His disciples, our Lord alludes to Himself as the unique mediator between God and humanity (cf. Jn 1:51)."
"As His disciples today," Pope Leo went on to underscore, "we know that Jesus is not only the source of our communion with God, but also with one another."
The Holy Father reminded the Assembly participants that in his Encyclical Magnifica humanitas, on safeguarding the human person in the time of artificial intelligence, he wrote that "Christian solidarity finds its source in the mystery of Christ and emerges from our communion in the sacraments, particularly the Eucharist."
An ever greater sign of Godâs presence in your various countries
"For this reason," Pope Leo urged, "I would like to encourage you to continue to promote a Eucharistic spirituality within your local Churches, that is, a spirituality of ecclesial unity grounded in the charity that flows from the gift of our Lord in the Eucharist."
"In this way," he exhorted, "it is my hope that the bonds of communion within and between the local Churches will be strengthened and become an ever greater sign of Godâs presence in your various countries, which in turn will help you be bridge-builders together throughout Asia."
Finally, the Holy Father concluded by commending all gathered, and their deliberations, to the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of the Church, before invoking upon them the Lordâs gifts of wisdom and fortitude.
"And may the blessing of Almighty God, the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit come down on you and remain with you for ever. Amen."
Thank you for reading our article. You can keep up-to-date by subscribing to our daily newsletter. Just click here.

items.body_text:
Cardinal Grech looks at the synodal journey for the Church in Asia
Vatican News
"It is not a matter of talking about synodality, but of seeking how to live it in the ordinary life of our Churches." With these words, Cardinal Mario Grech, Secretary General of the Synod of Bishops, outlined the fundamental perspective for the post-synodal phase on synodality which is the central role of the local Churches. He was addressing participants at the 12th Plenary Assembly of the Federation of Asian Bishops' Conferences (FABC) taking place in Jakarta, Indonesia, until Sunday July 26.
"The subject of the implementation phase and of the path of the Assemblies is, first of all, the local Church," the Cardinal said on Friday, July 24, emphasizing that this statement is not merely organizational in nature. Far from being simply an administrative subdivision of the universal Church, the local Church is, Cardinal Grech said, "a true manifestation of the Church in a particular place, where the Gospel is pro-claimed, the sacraments are celebrated, and the faithful are gathered into com-munion with Christ."
Sharing gifts, experiences and witness
In his address to the Assembly, focusing on the theme, "The Call to Synodal Conversion and the Mission to Be Bridges and Bridge-Builders in Asia", the Secretary General of the Synod recalled that the universal Church cannot be understood as an abstract reality separated from the concrete communities in which it lives. "If a local church fails to contribute, it deprives the universal Church of something vital," he explained, because every particular Church brings with it "unique gifts, experiences, resources, and a distinct witness that God intends to enrich the whole body of Christ."
Reflecting on the synodal journey launched in 2021, Cardinal Grech recalled the guiding question behind the process: How can we reach the People of God? From this starting point came a deliberate choice: "The participation of all could not merely be the content; it had first of all to be the method. Likewise, the People of God could not simply be the object; above all, they had to be the subject of the journey." Therefore, "to listen to the Churchâand this has fundamentally been our intention, since 'a synodal Church is a Church which listens'âmeans, concretely, to listen to the Churches."
Strengthening communion and supporting mission
Cardinal Grech then highlighted the importance of reciprocity among the Churches, which are called to share their experiences and gifts. The synodal process, he explained, is not primarily aimed at producing new texts, but at fostering "a circulation of gifts that strengthens communion and supports the mission."
One of the innovations that emerged from the synodal journey was what he called the restitutio - continuous feedback: every stage of the process was returned to the local communities so that it could be received and reflected upon anew. "The movement was therefore no longer unidirectional, but bidirectionalâindeed, circular," Cardinal Grech said. This approach was necessary to ensure that the synodal process remained closely connected to the real life of the communities: "Only by listening and listening anew to the local Churchesâthat is, to the People of God 'in flesh and blood', made up of baptized men and womenâcould there be sufficient assurance that the work of a restricted number of 'experts', even if they were members of the Ordinary General Assembly of the Synod of Bishops, would not simply âsteamrollâ the ecclesial grassroots."
Unique experience of Church in Asia
Addressing the Church in Asia in particular, the Cardinal emphasized the significance of its experience. Dialogue with other religions, cultural diversity, the often minority status of Christians, and closeness to the poor are all places where the Holy Spirit continues to be at work. items.summary: In an interview with Vatican Media, Cardinal Tarcisius Isao Kikuchi of Tokyo, Secretary General of the Federation of Asian Bishops' Conferences, reflects on the fruits of the FABC Plenary Assembly, highlighting faith, the protection of human dignity, and an urgent pastoral response to migration as shared priorities for the Church across Asia. Read all
items.body_text:
Cardinal Kikuchi of Tokyo: 'Church in Asia lives diverse realities, but one faith'
By Deborah Castellano Lubov
"Through these three days, we had the opportunity to deepen our understanding of our own reality in Asia and our understanding that we exist across really diverse realities but are united in one faith, one Body of Christ."
 
Cardinal Tarcisius Isao Kikuchi, SVD, Archbishop of Tokyo and Secretary General of the FABC, expressed this as he reflected on the FABC Plenary Assembly which opened on Monday in Jakarta, Indonesia, and concludes Sunday, in an interview with Vatican News. More than 120 Cardinals and Bishops from across Asia have gathered to pray and reflect on the Church's mission across the continent.
Cardinal Kikuchi presided over the Eucharistic Celebration on the Assembly's opening day. The days have been full of mutual sharing, and, on Thursday, delegates participating in the Assembly presented the results of their table discussions.
As the plenary continues, Vatican News spoke with the Archbishop of Tokyo about the Assembly, but also about the Church in Japan, and Pope Leo XIV's encyclical Magnifica humanitas.
Q: Your Eminence, what do you see as the main fruits of the FABC Plenary Assembly so far? What have been the principal themes and priorities of your discussions?
Cardinal Kikuchi: The Church in Asia exists in the diverse realities of culture, language, politics and economy, but one thing is common among most of us: we are an absolute minority in society, except in the Philippines. So far, we have only had three days, from Tuesday to Thursday, of reflection and sharing our experiences. We had members share three-minute video presentations on the first day, a day of prayer and Conversation in the Spirit led by Cardinal Tagle on Wednesday, and on Thursday, a day of learning about the changing socio-political landscape of Asia and sharing the reality of our local Churches.
Through these three days, we had the opportunity to deepen our understanding of our own reality in Asia and to deepen our awareness that we live in really diverse realities but are united in one faith, one Body of Christ. We shared the challenges and opportunities for mission based on local realities and found some common elements, especially the importance of dialogue. We are searching for the best way to be bridges ourselves, but also bridge-builders among people and together with people through dialogueâwith diverse cultures, with people, especially the poor, amid the diverse reality of numerous religions and in responding to the ecological crisis.
Q: Asia is an extraordinarily diverse continent. What have you learned from your brother Bishops during this assembly?
Drastic waves of migration in Asia call for immediate pastoral attention in many countries. Also, the protection of human dignity is a priority in many countries. Though each country has its own situation and problems, we can seek ways of cooperation among the Church communities in Asia. What the respective Church communities in Asia need is mutual understanding of each other's realities and mutual cooperation. All my brother Bishops, despite their diverse realities, are asking for recognition of their circumstances and for support, especially spiritual support, from one another.
Q: Catholics in Japan make up a relatively small percentage of the population. As Archbishop of Tokyo, how do you believe these days' deliberations will help your Church better witness or even spread the faith in this context?
According to official Church statistics, there are fewer than half a million Catholics in Japan. However, in reality, there are at least another half a million migrant Catholics in the country. The official registration system of the Church in Japan does not fully account for these migrant Catholics. For example, there are an estimated 40,000 Filipinos residing within the Archdiocese of Tokyo, and many young Vietnamese working in Japan on temporary visas are also Catholic.

items.title: How classical education can be an antidote to AI
items.summary: (RNS) — AI is more likely to harm education than help it. Classical education will become ever more relevant.
items.body_text:
How classical education can be an antidote to AI
(RNS) — In his 1939 essay “Learning in Wartime,” C.S. Lewis posed the question of whether it was still worthwhile to study while one’s country was at war. His audience was full of young men with a sense of foreboding for the safety of their country, the lives of their friends serving in the army and their own possible enlistment.
As a Christian thinker, Lewis answered in the affirmative, arguing that it was very appropriate for men to continue their studies while they could. “Life has never been normal,” Lewis writes, and therefore, the belief that education should occur only in times of normalcy is unfounded. No war can ever eradicate our pursuit of truth, meaning and happiness. Therefore, he argues, these should be pursued vigorously, even during times of imminent danger.
The advent of artificial intelligence brings similar feelings of foreboding and disruption. Some Americans fear they might lose their jobs to AI. Teachers, parents and administrators are urgently discussing how AI might change the classroom. Some view AI as a harbinger of welcome efficiency, whereby students can avoid the thankless grunt work of memorization and other tasks, enabling them to use their newfound time for more creative output. Others fear that AI could unleash a lazier, less literate society, more dependent on technology and less likely to engage in independent thinking.
While the future remains unknown, I’m more inclined to credit the less optimistic AI prediction.
I do not fear AI, nor do I doubt that AI can have some benefits. But I think AI is more likely to harm education than help it, even if it is used simply as a supplementary tool to a traditional education, and I fear the level of trust some are placing in it. There are certain educational pillars for the young — such as grammar, memorization, composition, recitation, discipline, endurance and the general trial and error of solving a problem — that reliance on AI and its shortcuts is likely to weaken.
In this time of uncertainty, we should look to Lewis as our guide. Lewis’ defense of education was not antiquarian. He didn’t encourage his students to continue their studies simply because that was what previous generations had done. He wanted his audience to continue learning because it was better for their souls. Centered on the pursuit of the true, the good and the beautiful — a reflection of God’s own nature — genuine education was directed to a higher end. If his students were to be drafted, and the prospect of death loomed even larger, then they would be able to face death armed with a good education. To Lewis, this meant a classical education.
In its substance, classical education consists of the seven liberal arts: the trivium of grammar, logic and rhetoric and the quadrivium of arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy. Grammar describes the world through the symbols we call words, making all the arts communicable. Logic disciplines our reason to decipher between true and false, so that we can make rational, rather than emotional, decisions. Rhetoric teaches us how to persuade, so that we can engage in political life civilly and peaceably. The quadrivium, meanwhile, explores number, space, harmony and order, coming to know reality in its truth, goodness and beauty through essential, knowable structure.
In its aims and essentials, classical education is the best that a student can receive. It is a comprehensive education because it consists of both a distinct perspective on human nature alongside a sophisticated, matching framework for the liberal arts. Classical education upholds an objective reality knowable through human reason. It affirms a right and a wrong, a good and a bad, a true and a false. Ideally, it inspires virtue through the witness of moral teachers and through a culture that habituates students to courage, moderation, prudence and justice.
